title: Rust: From Zero to Confident
summary: A serious, guided course in Rust that takes you from your very first line of code to the ideas that make Rust special. You read a short concept, build muscle memory by typing small, complete programs along with the tutor — every line explained — and then apply what you learned in a graded challenge whose hidden tests decide correctness. Nine foundation units of steadily rising difficulty — from printing a line to ownership, collections, your own types, and error handling. Then an intermediate Database track using SQLite via the `rusqlite` crate: connecting and querying, transactions and atomicity, WAL mode with connection pools, the N+1 query problem, pagination, and indexes with query plans — followed by an advanced track on Rust's type system: traits, generics, trait bounds, associated types, static vs dynamic dispatch, lifetimes, and Send/Sync with object safety. Then an advanced concurrency track — threads, channels, shared state with Arc/Mutex, and data parallelism — and a data structures & algorithms track: stacks and queues, linked lists, maps and sets, binary search trees, sorting and searching, and recursion with dynamic programming. Almost everything runs on the standard library alone — only the Database track pulls in the `rusqlite` crate. No prior Rust needed.

units.title: Hello & printing
units.intro:
Your very first steps in Rust: what a program is, how to print to the screen,
how to name a value, and how to call a function. By the end you will write a
tiny greeting function and let the tests check it.

steps.title: What a Rust program is
steps.intro:
Before you write anything, picture what a computer actually does: it loads your
compiled program into memory and starts executing machine instructions one after
another. A program needs a single, agreed-upon place to begin — in Rust that
place is the function `main`. The operating system hands control to your program,
Rust runs `main` top to bottom, and anything you print travels to a stream called
**standard output** (stdout), which the terminal shows on screen. This first
concept makes that model concrete so the code that follows is never a mystery.
steps.body:
## A program starts at `main`

Every Rust program begins running at a special function called **`main`**.
Think of it as the front door: when you run your program, Rust walks in through
`main` and does, top to bottom, whatever it finds there.

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
```

Three things to notice:

- **`fn main() { ... }`** declares the `main` function. `fn` means *function*;
  the `{ }` hold its body.
- **`println!`** prints a line of text to the screen. The `!` tells you it is a
  **macro**, not a regular function — for now, just know it prints.
- The text in **`"..."`** is a *string*: the exact characters to print.

In the next steps you will type small, complete programs yourself. When your
code matches the target, the tutor runs it so you can see the output — that is
how you build muscle memory.

steps.title: Print your first line
steps.intro:
This drill cements the one skeleton every Rust program shares. Under the hood,
`println!` is a macro the compiler expands into code that formats your text and
writes the resulting bytes to standard output, with a trailing newline. There is
no loop and no branching here — just the entry point `main` and a single write to
the screen.
steps.prompt:
Type the classic first program. It prints a single line and stops.

**Why:** this cements the shape every Rust program shares — a `main` function
and a `println!` that writes one line. Reproduce it exactly, character for
character.
line_comments: Declares `main`, the function Rust runs first; `{` opens its body.
Prints the text `Hello, world!` followed by a newline to standard output.
Closes the body of `main`; when execution reaches here the program ends.
steps.explanation:
That is a complete Rust program. Rust entered `main`, ran the one `println!`,
printed `Hello, world!`, and then `main` ended — so the program finished. Every
program you write grows from exactly this skeleton.

steps.title: Print two lines in order
steps.intro:
Programs run top to bottom. Two `println!` calls run in the order you write
them, each writing its own line and its own trailing newline. Seeing the output
appear in source order makes the "instructions run in sequence" model concrete.
steps.prompt:
Print two separate lines. The order of the statements is the order of the
output.

**Why:** statements execute top to bottom. Each `println!` writes one line, so
the first call's text appears above the second's.
line_comments: Runs first: prints `Learning Rust` on its own line.
Runs next: prints `One line at a time` below the first line.
Closes `main`; the program ends after both lines have printed.
steps.explanation:
The two `println!` calls ran in source order, so `Learning Rust` printed first
and `One line at a time` second. That top-to-bottom flow is the backbone of every
program.

steps.title: Name a value and print it
steps.intro:
Here you meet the idea of a **variable**: a name bound to a value living in
memory. `let name = "Rust";` reserves a slot and labels it `name`. Then string
**interpolation** — writing `{name}` inside the text — tells `println!` to look
up the variable and splice its value into the output at that exact spot.
steps.prompt:
Give a value a name with `let`, then print it *inside* the text.

**Why:** `let name = "Rust";` creates a variable called `name`. Writing
`{name}` inside the string drops the variable's value right there — this is
**interpolation**. Type the program exactly.
line_comments: Binds the name `name` to the text `"Rust"`; `let` creates the variable.
Prints `Hello, Rust!` — `{name}` is replaced by the variable's value.
steps.explanation:
`let name = "Rust";` bound the name `name` to the text `Rust`, and
`println!("Hello, {name}!")` substituted that value into the `{name}` slot, so
the program printed `Hello, Rust!`. Variables let you say a value once and reuse
it by name.

steps.title: Implement greet
steps.intro:
Now you apply everything, and one new idea matters: the difference between
borrowing text and owning it. The parameter `name: &str` is a **string slice** —
a borrowed, read-only view into text the caller still owns. The return type
`String` is **owned** text your function builds fresh and hands back. The
`format!` macro does exactly that: it allocates a new `String` and copies the
fixed parts plus `name` into it. Hidden tests, not the screen, decide correctness.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `greet`:

```rust
pub fn greet(name: &str) -> String { ... }
```

It takes a name (a string slice `&str`) and returns a `String` that reads
`Hello, {name}!`.

Examples:

- `greet("World")` → `"Hello, World!"`
- `greet("Rust")` → `"Hello, Rust!"`

**Hint:** the `format!` macro builds a `String` the same way `println!` builds a
printed line — with `{name}` interpolation.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
`format!` copies the fixed text `Hello, ` and `!` plus the `n` characters of
`name` into a fresh `String`. The work and the memory both grow in direct
proportion to the length of `name`, so the time is **O(n)** and the space is
**O(n)**, where `n` is the length of the name. There is no hidden loop — it is a
single pass that builds the result once.

units.title: Variables & types
units.intro:
Every value in Rust has a **type** the compiler tracks for you: whole numbers,
real numbers, booleans, text. You will meet immutability (the default), the
`mut` keyword that opts into change, and simple arithmetic. By the end you will
convert a temperature with a graded challenge.

steps.title: Values have types
steps.intro:
A type is a promise about what a value is and what you can do with it. The
compiler uses types to catch mistakes before your program ever runs — adding a
number to a piece of text is simply rejected. Most of the time Rust *infers* the
type from the value, so you rarely write it, but it is always there.
steps.body:
## Numbers, booleans, and text

Common types you will use immediately:

- **`i32`** — a 32-bit signed integer, the default whole number (`let n = 42;`).
- **`f64`** — a 64-bit floating-point number, for reals (`let pi = 3.14;`).
- **`bool`** — either `true` or `false`.
- **`&str`** / **`String`** — borrowed text / owned text.

Bindings are **immutable by default**:

```rust
let x = 5;
// x = 6; // error: cannot assign twice to immutable `x`
let mut y = 5;
y = 6;     // fine: `mut` opts in to change
```

Immutability by default is a safety feature: a value you did not mark `mut`
cannot change under you. You reach for `mut` only when you truly need it.

steps.title: Integer arithmetic
steps.intro:
Integers support the usual arithmetic. Here you bind two whole numbers and print
their sum. `{}` is a positional slot: the arguments after the string fill the
slots left to right. The compiler infers both variables are `i32`.
steps.prompt:
Bind two numbers, add them, and print the result using positional `{}` slots.

**Why:** arithmetic on integers is immediate. The `{}` slots are filled by the
arguments after the string, in order.
line_comments: Prints `7 + 5 = 12`; the three `{}` slots take `a`, `b`, and `a + b` in order.
steps.explanation:
The three `{}` slots were filled, in order, by `a`, `b`, and the computed value
`a + b`, so the line read `7 + 5 = 12`. The addition happened right inside the
argument list.

steps.title: Change a mutable variable
steps.intro:
A binding marked `mut` may be reassigned or updated. `count += 1` is shorthand
for `count = count + 1`. Watching the value before and after makes mutation
concrete: the same slot in memory now holds a different number.
steps.prompt:
Create a mutable counter, increment it, and print it before and after.

**Why:** only a `mut` binding may change. `count += 1` adds one in place. Without
`mut`, the second assignment would be a compile error.
line_comments: Binds a **mutable** variable `count` to `0`; `mut` allows later change.
Adds one to `count` in place; `+=` is `count = count + 1`.
steps.explanation:
Because `count` was declared `mut`, `count += 1` was allowed and updated the
value from `0` to `1`. The two prints showed the before and after. Remove `mut`
and Rust would refuse to compile the reassignment — that is immutability
protecting you by default.

steps.title: A boolean from a comparison
steps.intro:
Comparisons like `>` produce a `bool` — exactly `true` or `false`. Storing that
result in a variable shows that a boolean is an ordinary value you can name,
print, and later use to make decisions.
steps.prompt:
Compare two numbers, store the resulting `bool`, and print it.

**Why:** `a > b` evaluates to a `bool`. Booleans are plain values you can bind
with `let` and print like any other.
line_comments: Evaluates `a > b` (which is `true`) and binds that `bool` to `bigger`.
steps.explanation:
`a > b` compared the two numbers and produced the boolean `true`, which you
stored in `bigger` and printed. Comparisons are how programs turn data into the
yes/no decisions you will branch on in the next unit.

steps.title: Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit
steps.intro:
You apply typed arithmetic. The formula is `F = C * 9/5 + 32`. Working in `f64`
matters: if you divided integers, `9/5` would truncate to `1` and the answer
would be wrong. Using floating-point literals (`9.0`, `5.0`, `32.0`) keeps the
fraction exact.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `celsius_to_fahrenheit`:

```rust
pub fn celsius_to_fahrenheit(c: f64) -> f64 { ... }
```

Return the temperature in Fahrenheit using `F = C * 9/5 + 32`.

Examples:

- `celsius_to_fahrenheit(0.0)` → `32.0`
- `celsius_to_fahrenheit(100.0)` → `212.0`
- `celsius_to_fahrenheit(-40.0)` → `-40.0`

**Hint:** use floating-point literals (`9.0`, `5.0`, `32.0`) so the division
does not truncate.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The function does a fixed number of arithmetic operations — one multiply, one
divide, one add — regardless of the input value. There is no loop and no
allocation, so both time and space are constant: **O(1)**. Using `f64` literals
keeps `9.0 / 5.0` as `1.8` instead of truncating to `1`.

units.title: Control flow: if/else & match
units.intro:
Programs make decisions. `if`/`else` chooses between paths based on a boolean,
and because `if` is an **expression** in Rust it can even produce a value.
`match` compares a value against patterns and runs the first that fits. By the
end you will classify a number's sign under hidden tests.

steps.title: Choosing a path
steps.intro:
A branch is a fork in the road: the program evaluates a condition and takes one
way or the other. In Rust `if` is not just a statement — it is an expression that
evaluates to a value, so you can assign the chosen branch directly. `match` is
the exhaustive cousin: it forces you to handle every possibility, which is how
Rust stops you forgetting a case.

steps.title: Branch with if/else
steps.intro:
This drill takes one path or the other depending on a condition. The `%`
operator gives the remainder of a division; `n % 2 == 0` is the classic test for
an even number. Exactly one of the two blocks runs.
steps.prompt:
Print whether a number is even or odd using `if`/`else`.

**Why:** `n % 2` is the remainder after dividing by 2; it is `0` for even
numbers. The `if` runs one block, the `else` the other — never both.
line_comments: Tests the condition `n % 2 == 0`; the remainder of 7 / 2 is 1, so this is false.
The `if` block — would print `is even` — is skipped because the condition was false.
The `else` block runs instead, printing `7 is odd`.
steps.explanation:
`7 % 2` is `1`, so the condition `== 0` was `false` and Rust took the `else`
path, printing `7 is odd`. Exactly one branch runs; change `n` to an even number
and the other block would run instead.

steps.title: if as an expression
steps.intro:
In Rust `if` yields a value, so you can bind the chosen branch straight to a
variable. Each arm's final expression (no semicolon) is its value, and both arms
must have the same type. This removes the need for a throwaway mutable variable.
steps.prompt:
Use `if`/`else` as an expression to choose a label, then print it.

**Why:** `if cond { a } else { b }` evaluates to `a` or `b`. Binding it with
`let` is cleaner than mutating a variable afterwards.
line_comments: `if` is an expression: it evaluates to `"even"` (since 4 is even) and binds it to `label`.
steps.explanation:
The `if`/`else` expression evaluated to `"even"` and that value was bound to
`label` in one step. Using `if` as an expression keeps the code direct — no
temporary `mut` variable needed.

steps.title: Match on a value
steps.intro:
`match` lines a value up against patterns and runs the first arm that fits. The
final `_` arm is the catch-all, which also makes the match **exhaustive** — Rust
checks that every possible value is covered. Here it names small numbers and
calls everything else `many`.
steps.prompt:
Use `match` to turn a number into a word.

**Why:** `match` picks the first matching arm. The `_` arm catches every other
value, so the match covers all cases — Rust requires that.
line_comments: Starts a `match` on `n`; its result is bound to `word`.
Arm: if `n` is `0`, the value is `"zero"`.
Arm: if `n` is `1`, the value is `"one"`.
Arm: `n` is `2`, so this arm matches and `word` becomes `"two"`.
Catch-all `_` arm: any other value would be `"many"`.
Closes the `match` expression (note the trailing semicolon on the `let`).
steps.explanation:
`match n` tried the arms top to bottom and `2 => "two"` fit, so `word` became
`"two"`. The `_` arm guarantees every possible number is handled, which is why
the compiler accepts the match as complete.

steps.title: Classify a number's sign
steps.intro:
You apply branching. The function returns one of three fixed words, so the return
type is `&'static str` — a borrowed view into text baked into the program itself,
which is why no `String` allocation is needed. An `if`/`else if`/`else` chain, or
a `match` guard, picks the right one.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `sign`:

```rust
pub fn sign(n: i32) -> &'static str { ... }
```

Return:

- `"negative"` when `n < 0`
- `"zero"` when `n == 0`
- `"positive"` when `n > 0`

Examples:

- `sign(-5)` → `"negative"`
- `sign(0)` → `"zero"`
- `sign(7)` → `"positive"`

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The function performs at most two comparisons and returns a reference to a string
literal already stored in the program's binary. There is no loop and no
allocation, so time and space are both constant: **O(1)**. `&'static str` means
the returned text lives for the whole program, so nothing is created or copied.

units.title: Loops
units.intro:
Repetition is where computers earn their keep. `for` walks every item of a range
or collection, `while` repeats until a condition changes, and `loop` runs until
you `break`. By the end you will sum the numbers from 1 to n under hidden tests.

steps.title: Doing something many times
steps.intro:
A loop is a controlled way to repeat work without copying code. The computer
keeps a small piece of state — a counter, or the loop's position in a range — and
repeats the body, updating that state each pass, until a stopping condition is
met. Choosing the right loop is about who controls the stopping: the range (`for`),
a condition (`while`), or your own `break` (`loop`).

steps.title: Count with a for loop
steps.intro:
A `for` over a range binds each value in turn to the loop variable and runs the
body once per value. `1..=3` is an **inclusive** range, so it yields 1, 2, and 3.
The loop variable is fresh each pass; you do not manage a counter by hand.
steps.prompt:
Print the numbers 1, 2, 3 with a `for` loop over an inclusive range.

**Why:** `1..=3` yields 1, 2, 3 (the `=` includes the end). The body runs once
per value, with `i` bound to that value.
line_comments: Loops over the inclusive range `1..=3`, binding `i` to 1, then 2, then 3.
steps.explanation:
The `for` loop ran its body three times, with `i` taking the values 1, 2, 3 from
the inclusive range `1..=3`, so it printed three lines. The loop variable was
managed for you — no counter to increment, no condition to get wrong.

steps.title: Count down with while
steps.intro:
A `while` loop checks its condition **before** each pass and stops when it turns
false. You must change the state the condition depends on inside the body, or the
loop never ends. Here the countdown decrements `n` until it reaches zero.
steps.prompt:
Count down from 3 to 1 with a `while` loop.

**Why:** `while n > 0` keeps looping as long as the condition holds. You must
change `n` inside the body (here with `n -= 1`) so it eventually stops.
line_comments: Binds a mutable `n` to `3` — mutable because the loop will change it.
Checks `n > 0` before each pass; loops while it holds.
Body: prints the current value of `n`.
Decrements `n` by one; without this the loop would run forever.
Closes the `while` body; control jumps back to re-check the condition.
Runs after the loop ends (when `n` reached 0): prints `liftoff`.
steps.explanation:
The loop printed 3, 2, 1 — one per pass — and stopped when `n` reached `0` and
the condition `n > 0` became false. Then `liftoff` printed. The `n -= 1` is what
makes the loop terminate; forget it and the condition would stay true forever.

steps.title: Accumulate a running total
steps.intro:
The accumulator pattern is everywhere: keep a running value outside the loop and
update it each pass. Here `sum` starts at zero and grows by each `i`. This is
exactly the shape of the challenge that ends this unit.
steps.prompt:
Add the numbers 1 through 5 into a running total and print it.

**Why:** the accumulator pattern — a `mut` total updated each pass — turns
repetition into a single computed result.
line_comments: Loops over `1..=5`, binding `i` to each value in turn.
Adds the current `i` to `sum`; after the loop `sum` holds 1+2+3+4+5.
steps.explanation:
Each pass added `i` to `sum`, so after walking 1 through 5 the total was `15`.
Keeping an accumulator outside the loop and updating it inside is the core idea
behind the `sum_to` challenge coming next.

steps.title: Sum from 1 to n
steps.intro:
You apply the accumulator pattern. Return the sum `1 + 2 + ... + n`, and `0` when
`n` is `0`. Use `u32` (unsigned) because the inputs and the total are never
negative. A single `for` over an inclusive range, adding into a running total,
solves it in one linear pass.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `sum_to`:

```rust
pub fn sum_to(n: u32) -> u32 { ... }
```

Return the sum of all integers from `1` to `n` inclusive. `sum_to(0)` is `0`.

Examples:

- `sum_to(0)` → `0`
- `sum_to(5)` → `15`
- `sum_to(100)` → `5050`

**Hint:** start a total at `0` and add each value from a `for i in 1..=n` loop.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The loop runs exactly `n` times, doing constant work each pass, so the time grows
in direct proportion to `n`: **O(n)**. Only one accumulator variable is kept
regardless of `n`, so the space is **O(1)**. (A closed form `n*(n+1)/2` would be
O(1) time, but the loop version is what this unit teaches and is plenty fast.)

units.title: Functions
units.intro:
Functions are how you name a piece of work and reuse it. You will pass arguments,
return values, and compose small functions into bigger ones. By the end you will
compute the maximum of three numbers under hidden tests.

steps.title: Named, reusable work
steps.intro:
When `main` calls a function, the computer sets up a small region of memory — a
**stack frame** — for that call: it copies the arguments into the parameters,
runs the body, and the return value flows back to the caller. A function has
typed inputs and a typed output, and in Rust the final expression without a
semicolon is what it hands back.
steps.body:
## Parameters, return values, composition

```rust
fn double(n: i32) -> i32 {
    n * 2          // tail expression, no semicolon → the return value
}

fn quadruple(n: i32) -> i32 {
    double(double(n)) // functions compose: the output of one feeds the next
}
```

- `(n: i32)` declares a parameter `n` of type `i32`.
- `-> i32` declares the return type.
- The last expression with **no semicolon** is returned; `return` is only needed
  to leave early.

Small, well-named functions are the building blocks of every program — you write
a calculation once and call it wherever you need it.

steps.title: Define a function and call it
steps.intro:
Here you declare your own function and call it from `main`. The argument `21` is
copied into the parameter `n`, the body computes `n * 2`, and that value flows
back to be stored in `result`. The tail expression `n * 2` has no semicolon, so
it is the return value.
steps.prompt:
Define `double` and call it from `main`.

**Why:** a function names a calculation. `double(21)` copies `21` into `n`,
returns `n * 2`, and you store the answer. The last expression (no semicolon) is
what the function returns.
line_comments: Declares `double`, taking an `i32` called `n` and returning an `i32`.
The tail expression `n * 2` (no semicolon) is the value returned.
Calls `double(21)`; `21` is copied into `n`, and the returned `42` is bound to `result`.
steps.explanation:
`main` called `double(21)`, which computed `21 * 2` and returned `42`; you stored
it in `result` and printed it. The blank line between the two functions is just
for readability — Rust ignores it.

steps.title: Compose two functions
steps.intro:
Functions compose: the output of one can be the input of another. `min` and `max`
are methods already on `i32`, called with a dot. Here you build `clamp_small` on
top of them, then call it from `main`. This is how larger behaviour is assembled
from small, tested pieces.
steps.prompt:
Write `clamp_small` that keeps a number within 0..=9, built on the `max` and
`min` methods, then call it.

**Why:** `n.max(0)` is never below 0; `.min(9)` is never above 9. Chaining them
clamps the value — and wrapping that in a named function makes it reusable.
line_comments: `n.max(0)` lifts anything below 0 up to 0, then `.min(9)` caps it at 9; the result is returned.
Calls `clamp_small(15)`; 15 is capped to 9, which prints.
Calls `clamp_small(-4)`; -4 is lifted to 0, which prints.
steps.explanation:
`clamp_small` chained the `max` and `min` methods to keep its input within 0..=9,
so `15` became `9` and `-4` became `0`. You composed two existing operations into
one named function and reused it twice.

steps.title: Maximum of three
steps.intro:
You apply functions and comparison. Return the largest of three `i32` values.
The cleanest way reuses the `max` method twice — `a.max(b).max(c)` — but an
`if`/`else` chain works too. The point is to return the right value, not to print
it; hidden tests check it.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `max_of_three`:

```rust
pub fn max_of_three(a: i32, b: i32, c: i32) -> i32 { ... }
```

Return the largest of the three values.

Examples:

- `max_of_three(1, 2, 3)` → `3`
- `max_of_three(9, -4, 0)` → `9`
- `max_of_three(5, 5, 5)` → `5`

**Hint:** `a.max(b)` returns the larger of `a` and `b`; chain it with `.max(c)`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The function does a fixed number of comparisons — two — no matter what the inputs
are, and keeps no extra data. Both time and space are therefore constant:
**O(1)**. `a.max(b)` yields the larger of the first two, and `.max(c)` folds in
the third.

units.title: Ownership & borrowing
units.intro:
Here is the idea at the heart of Rust: every value has a single **owner**, and
when the owner goes out of scope the value is freed — no garbage collector, no
manual free. Instead of giving ownership away, you can **borrow** a value with
`&`. By the end you will count characters in borrowed text under hidden tests.

steps.title: Owning and borrowing values
steps.intro:
Memory safety usually costs you either a garbage collector (pauses, overhead) or
manual `free` calls (bugs, crashes). Rust takes a third path: the compiler tracks,
at compile time, who owns each value and frees it exactly once when the owner
leaves scope. Borrowing lets other code read or mutate a value temporarily
without taking that ownership — all checked before your program runs.
steps.body:
## Move, borrow, and scope

A `String` has a single owner. Assigning it **moves** ownership; the old name can
no longer be used:

```rust
let a = String::from("hi");
let b = a;        // ownership moves to `b`
// println!("{a}"); // error: `a` was moved
```

**Borrowing** with `&` lends access without moving:

```rust
fn len(s: &String) -> usize { s.len() } // borrows, does not own
let a = String::from("hi");
let n = len(&a);  // lend a reference
println!("{a}");  // still usable — ownership never left
```

A `&` is a shared, read-only borrow; `&mut` is an exclusive borrow that may
mutate. The rule — many readers **or** one writer, never both — is what makes
data races impossible. When the owner's scope ends, the value is freed
automatically.

steps.title: Borrow instead of move
steps.intro:
Passing `&s` lends a reference to the function instead of handing over ownership,
so `s` is still usable afterwards. The function reads through the borrow with
`.len()` and returns a number. Nothing was copied or freed; the owner stayed put.
steps.prompt:
Pass a borrow of a `String` to a function that reads its length, then keep using
the original.

**Why:** `&s` lends a read-only reference. Because ownership never moved, `s`
remains valid after the call — borrowing is how functions look without taking.
line_comments: Declares `char_len`, borrowing a `String` by shared reference `&String`.
Reads the length through the borrow and returns it; the caller keeps ownership.
Lends a reference with `&s`; the returned length is bound to `n`.
Prints `hello has 5 bytes` — `s` is still usable because it was only borrowed.
Closes `main`; `s` goes out of scope here and its memory is freed automatically.
steps.explanation:
`char_len(&s)` borrowed `s` rather than taking it, so after the call `s` was
still valid and printable. The `&` is the whole point: the function looked at the
data without owning it, and Rust freed `s` only when `main` ended.

steps.title: Mutate through a borrow
steps.intro:
A `&mut` borrow lends **exclusive** write access. The function can change the
value in place, and the change is visible to the owner afterwards. While a `&mut`
borrow is active, no other borrow of the same value may exist — that exclusivity
is what prevents data races.
steps.prompt:
Pass a mutable borrow so a function can append to a `String` in place.

**Why:** `&mut s` lends exclusive write access. `push_str` appends through the
borrow, and the owner sees the change once the borrow ends.
line_comments: Declares `add_bang`, taking an exclusive mutable borrow `&mut String`.
Appends `"!"` to the borrowed string in place; no value is returned.
Creates a mutable `String` `s` holding `"hi"` — mutable so it can be borrowed `&mut`.
Lends an exclusive borrow with `&mut s`; the function mutates it.
Prints `hi!` — the append is visible to the owner now the borrow has ended.
steps.explanation:
`add_bang(&mut s)` borrowed `s` exclusively and appended through that borrow, so
afterwards `s` read `hi!`. Only one `&mut` borrow may exist at a time — that
exclusivity is exactly what makes in-place mutation safe in Rust.

steps.title: Borrow text as &str
steps.intro:
A `&str` is a borrowed, read-only view of UTF-8 text. Both a string literal and
an owned `String` can be viewed as `&str`, so functions that only read text take
`&str` to accept either. Here `first_word` returns a slice that borrows *into*
the original — no new text is allocated.
steps.prompt:
Write a function taking `&str` that returns the first word, and call it with a
literal.

**Why:** `&str` is a borrowed view of text. Taking `&str` (not `String`) lets the
function accept literals and `String`s alike, without owning anything.
line_comments: Declares `first_word`, borrowing text as `&str` and returning a borrowed `&str`.
Splits on spaces, takes the first piece, and falls back to `""` if there is none.
Calls `first_word` with a string literal (itself a `&str`); binds the slice to `word`.
steps.explanation:
`first_word` viewed the text through a `&str` borrow and returned a slice that
points *into* the same text — no copy, no allocation. Taking `&str` is why it
accepted the literal directly; a `String` would have worked just as well.

steps.title: Count characters
steps.intro:
You apply borrowing. Take a `&str` — a borrowed view, so you never own or consume
the caller's text — and return how many **characters** it contains. Counting
`chars()` (not bytes) matters for text like `héllo`, where one accented letter is
a single character but more than one byte. The count is a `usize`.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `count_chars`:

```rust
pub fn count_chars(s: &str) -> usize { ... }
```

Return the number of Unicode characters in `s`.

Examples:

- `count_chars("")` → `0`
- `count_chars("abc")` → `3`
- `count_chars("héllo")` → `5`

**Hint:** `s.chars()` yields the characters; `.count()` counts them. Counting
bytes with `.len()` would be wrong for accented letters.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
`chars()` walks the string once, decoding each UTF-8 character, and `count()`
tallies them — a single linear pass over the `n` bytes of input, so the time is
**O(n)**. No collection is built; only a running count is kept, so the space is
**O(1)**. Because `s` is borrowed as `&str`, the caller's text is never owned or
copied.

units.title: Collections: Vec & HashMap
units.intro:
Real programs juggle many values at once. A `Vec<T>` is a growable list; a
`HashMap<K, V>` maps keys to values. You will build them, iterate them, and use
iterator methods like `filter` and `collect`. By the end you will extract the
even numbers from a slice under hidden tests.

steps.title: Lists and maps
steps.intro:
A collection stores many values behind one name and lets you add, read, and walk
them. A `Vec<T>` keeps its elements in order in a single block of memory, which
makes indexing and iteration fast. A `HashMap<K, V>` trades order for near-instant
lookup by key. Iterators tie them together: a uniform way to visit every element
and transform it without writing index loops by hand.
steps.body:
## `Vec`, `HashMap`, and iterators

A **`Vec<T>`** is a growable list:

```rust
let mut xs = vec![1, 2, 3];
xs.push(4);           // now [1, 2, 3, 4]
println!("{}", xs[0]); // index access: 1
```

A **`HashMap<K, V>`** maps keys to values:

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
let mut ages = HashMap::new();
ages.insert("Al", 30);
println!("{:?}", ages.get("Al")); // Some(30)
```

**Iterators** visit each element. `iter()` borrows the elements; adapters like
`filter` and `map` transform the stream lazily; `collect()` gathers the results:

```rust
let evens: Vec<i32> = (1..=6).filter(|n| n % 2 == 0).collect(); // [2, 4, 6]
```

steps.title: Build and walk a Vec
steps.intro:
A `Vec` starts empty or from the `vec!` macro and grows with `push`. A `for` loop
over `&xs` borrows each element in turn so the vector stays usable afterwards.
Here you build a small list and print each item.
steps.prompt:
Create a `Vec`, push a value, then print every element with a `for` loop.

**Why:** `vec![..]` builds a list; `push` appends; `for x in &xs` borrows each
element so the vector is not consumed.
line_comments: Builds a mutable `Vec` `xs` with `[10, 20]` using the `vec!` macro.
Appends `30` to the end; `xs` is now `[10, 20, 30]`.
Loops over `&xs`, borrowing each element as `x` without consuming the vector.
steps.explanation:
You built `[10, 20]`, pushed `30`, and the `for` over `&xs` borrowed each element
to print it. Iterating by reference (`&xs`) means the vector was not consumed —
you could keep using it after the loop.

steps.title: Look up values in a HashMap
steps.intro:
A `HashMap` stores key→value pairs and looks them up fast. `get` returns an
`Option`: `Some(value)` when the key is present, `None` when it is not — Rust's
way of making "might be missing" impossible to ignore. Here you insert two scores
and look one up.
steps.prompt:
Insert two entries into a `HashMap` and look one up. `get` returns an `Option`.

**Why:** a `HashMap` maps keys to values. `get` returns `Some(v)` if the key
exists or `None` otherwise, so a missing key can never be mistaken for a value.
line_comments: Brings `HashMap` into scope so it can be named without its full path.
Creates an empty, mutable `HashMap`; key and value types are inferred from use.
Looks up `"Al"` and prints `Some(90)`; `get` returns an `Option`.
steps.explanation:
The map stored two name→score pairs, and `get("Al")` returned `Some(90)`, printed
with the `{:?}` debug slot. Had you asked for a missing name, `get` would return
`None` — the `Option` forces you to acknowledge that a key might not be there.

steps.title: Transform with an iterator
steps.intro:
Iterator adapters build a pipeline: `iter()` produces a stream, `map` transforms
each element, and `collect` gathers the results into a new `Vec`. The pipeline is
lazy — nothing runs until `collect` pulls the values through. This is the idiom
you will use in the challenge.
steps.prompt:
Double every number in a list using `iter().map(...).collect()`.

**Why:** iterator adapters form a pipeline. `map` transforms each element and
`collect` gathers them into a new `Vec`. The closure `|n| n * 2` is the transform.
line_comments: Builds the list `[1, 2, 3]` and binds it to `xs`.
Borrows `xs`, maps each element through `|n| n * 2`, and collects into a new `Vec<i32>`.
steps.explanation:
`iter()` streamed the elements, `map(|n| n * 2)` doubled each, and `collect()`
gathered them into a brand-new `Vec`, leaving `xs` untouched. The type annotation
`Vec<i32>` told `collect` what to build. This map/collect pipeline is exactly the
shape of the `evens` challenge.

steps.title: Keep the even numbers
steps.intro:
You apply iterators and `Vec`. Take a borrowed slice `&[i32]` — a read-only view
of a run of integers — and return a new `Vec<i32>` containing only the even ones,
in their original order. The idiom is `iter().filter(...).collect()`: keep the
elements for which `n % 2 == 0`. Because the input is borrowed, the caller's data
is never consumed.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `evens`:

```rust
pub fn evens(nums: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32> { ... }
```

Return a `Vec<i32>` with only the even numbers of `nums`, keeping their order.

Examples:

- `evens(&[1, 2, 3, 4])` → `[2, 4]`
- `evens(&[])` → `[]`
- `evens(&[2, 4, 6])` → `[2, 4, 6]`
- `evens(&[1, 3, 5])` → `[]`

**Hint:** `nums.iter().copied().filter(|n| n % 2 == 0).collect()`. `copied()`
turns `&i32` references into owned `i32` values.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The iterator visits each of the `n` elements exactly once, testing `n % 2 == 0`
in constant time, so the time is **O(n)**. The result `Vec` holds at most `n`
elements, so the space is **O(n)** in the worst case (all even). The input is a
borrowed slice, so nothing of the caller's is consumed; `copied()` turns each
`&i32` into an owned `i32` for the new vector.

units.title: Structs & enums
units.intro:
Now you model your own data. A `struct` groups related fields into one named type;
an `enum` says a value is exactly one of a fixed set of variants. Methods attach
behaviour with `impl`. By the end you will compute the distance between two points
you modelled yourself, under hidden tests.

steps.title: Modelling your own types
steps.intro:
Built-in types take you only so far; real programs describe their own domain. A
`struct` bundles several fields into one value you can pass around as a unit — a
point, a user, a config. An `enum` captures a closed choice: a value is exactly
one variant, and `match` forces you to handle each. Together they let the type
system encode the rules of your problem so invalid states become unrepresentable.

steps.title: Define and use a struct
steps.intro:
A `struct` defines a new type with named fields. You create a value with the
`Name { field: value }` syntax and read fields with a dot. Here `Point` groups an
x and a y, and `main` builds one and prints its parts.
steps.prompt:
Define a `Point` struct, create one, and print its fields.

**Why:** a `struct` bundles related data under one type. You build it with
`Point { x: .., y: .. }` and read fields with `p.x` / `p.y`.
line_comments: Prints `(3, 4)` by reading the fields `p.x` and `p.y`.
steps.explanation:
You defined a `Point` type with two fields and built one with `Point { x: 3, y: 4 }`,
then read its fields with `p.x` and `p.y` to print `(3, 4)`. A struct lets you
carry related data as a single value.

steps.title: Add a method with impl
steps.intro:
An `impl` block attaches methods to a type. A method whose first parameter is
`&self` borrows the value it is called on, so it can read fields without taking
ownership. You call it with a dot, like `p.magnitude_squared()`.
steps.prompt:
Give `Point` a method that reads its own fields, then call it.

**Why:** `impl Point { fn ...(&self) }` attaches behaviour. `&self` borrows the
point so the method can read `self.x` and `self.y`. Call it with `p.method()`.
line_comments: Opens an `impl` block to attach methods to `Point`.
Declares a method `sum` that borrows the point via `&self` and returns an `i32`.
Returns the sum of the two fields.
steps.explanation:
The `impl Point` block attached a `sum` method that borrowed the point with
`&self` and added its fields, so `p.sum()` returned `7`. Methods keep behaviour
next to the data it works on, called with the familiar dot syntax.

steps.title: Match on an enum
steps.intro:
An `enum` value is exactly one variant. `match` destructures it, pulling any data
a variant carries into names you can use. Because `match` must cover every
variant, the compiler guarantees you never forget one — a missing arm is a compile
error, not a runtime surprise.
steps.prompt:
Define a small `enum`, then `match` on a value to describe it.

**Why:** an `enum` is a closed set of variants. `match` runs the arm for the
actual variant and binds any data it carries; covering every variant is required.
line_comments: Binds `light` to the `Green` variant (named with the `Light::` path).
Starts a `match` on `light`; its result is bound to `action`.
steps.explanation:
`light` was the `Green` variant, so the matching arm made `action` be `"go"`. The
`match` had to list every variant of `Light`, which is how Rust guarantees you
handle all cases — add a fourth variant and this code would stop compiling until
you handle it.

steps.title: Manhattan distance between points
steps.intro:
You model data and use it. First define a `Point` with public `x` and `y` fields
(the tests build points directly), then implement `manhattan`, the grid distance
`|ax - bx| + |ay - by|`. The `.abs()` method gives the absolute value. This proves
you can both declare a type and compute over it.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Define a `Point` and implement `manhattan`:

```rust
pub struct Point {
    pub x: i32,
    pub y: i32,
}

pub fn manhattan(a: Point, b: Point) -> i32 { ... }
```

Return the Manhattan (taxicab) distance: `|a.x - b.x| + |a.y - b.y|`.

Examples:

- `manhattan(Point { x: 0, y: 0 }, Point { x: 3, y: 4 })` → `7`
- `manhattan(Point { x: 1, y: 1 }, Point { x: 1, y: 1 })` → `0`
- `manhattan(Point { x: -2, y: 0 }, Point { x: 2, y: 0 })` → `4`

**Hint:** `(a.x - b.x).abs()` is the absolute horizontal gap; add the vertical one.

Both `Point` (with public fields) and `manhattan` must be public so the tests can
use them. Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The function reads four fields and does a fixed handful of subtractions, absolute
values, and one addition — the same work for any input, with no loop and no
allocation. Both time and space are therefore constant: **O(1)**. Public fields
on `Point` let the tests construct values directly.

units.title: Error handling: Option & Result
units.intro:
Rust has no `null` and no exceptions. Instead, "might be missing" is an `Option`
and "might fail" is a `Result`, both ordinary enums the compiler makes you handle.
By the end you will write safe division that returns `None` instead of crashing,
under hidden tests.

steps.title: Absence and failure as values
steps.intro:
Most languages signal "no value" with `null` and "it broke" with exceptions —
both easy to ignore until they crash you at runtime. Rust makes both explicit in
the type system. An `Option<T>` is `Some(value)` or `None`; a `Result<T, E>` is
`Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. Because they are enums, you cannot use the inner
value without first handling the empty or failing case — the compiler insists.
steps.body:
## `Option` and `Result`

**`Option<T>`** models a value that may be absent:

```rust
fn first(xs: &[i32]) -> Option<i32> {
    if xs.is_empty() { None } else { Some(xs[0]) }
}
```

**`Result<T, E>`** models an operation that may fail:

```rust
fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<i32, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    s.parse::<i32>() // Ok(n) or Err(..)
}
```

You unwrap them by **handling both cases**, usually with `match`:

```rust
match first(&xs) {
    Some(n) => println!("first is {n}"),
    None => println!("empty"),
}
```

There is no `null` to forget and no exception to swallow — absence and failure are
values you must deal with, which is why Rust programs crash so rarely.

## Shortcut: the `?` operator

Writing a full `match` just to pass a `None`/`Err` upward gets noisy. When your
function itself returns `Option`/`Result`, the **`?`** operator does it for you:
it unwraps the `Some`/`Ok` value, or **returns early** with the `None`/`Err`.

```rust
fn first_doubled(xs: &[i32]) -> Option<i32> {
    let first = xs.first()?; // None here → return None from the whole function
    Some(first * 2)
}
```

`?` only works inside a function whose return type fits (an `Option` in an
`Option`-returning function, a `Result` in a `Result`-returning one). It is pure
sugar for the `match` above — the same behaviour, far less code.

steps.title: Handle an Option with match
steps.intro:
`Option` is how Rust says "maybe nothing". A function returns `Some(value)` or
`None`, and `match` forces you to handle both arms before you can touch the inner
value. Here a lookup either finds a value or reports it is missing.
steps.prompt:
Write a function returning `Option<i32>`, then handle both arms with `match`.

**Why:** `Option` makes absence explicit. `match` must cover `Some(n)` and
`None`, so you can never use a missing value by accident.
line_comments: Declares `halve`, returning `Option<i32>` — a value that may be absent.
If `n` is even, the half exists...
Otherwise there is no clean half...
`Some(h)` arm: binds `h` to `5` and prints `half is 5`.
`None` arm: would print `not even` for an odd input.
steps.explanation:
`halve(10)` returned `Some(5)`, so the `Some(h)` arm ran, binding `h` to `5`. The
`match` required both arms, so the `None` possibility could not be ignored — pass
an odd number and the `None` arm would run instead. That is error handling as
ordinary, checked values.

steps.title: Handle a Result
steps.intro:
A `Result` is `Ok(value)` on success or `Err(e)` on failure. Parsing text into a
number is the classic example: it returns a `Result` because the text might not
be a number. `match` handles both outcomes; the failing case carries an error you
can inspect.
steps.prompt:
Parse a string to a number and handle both `Ok` and `Err` with `match`.

**Why:** operations that can fail return a `Result`. `match` on `Ok(n)` / `Err(_)`
forces you to deal with the failure instead of letting it crash the program.
line_comments: Parses `text` as an `i32`; `parse` returns a `Result`, matched here.
`Ok(n)` arm: parsing succeeded, so `n` is `42` and this prints `parsed 42`.
`Err(_)` arm: would run if the text were not a number (the `_` ignores the error).
steps.explanation:
`"42".parse::<i32>()` succeeded, returning `Ok(42)`, so the `Ok(n)` arm bound `n`
to `42` and printed `parsed 42`. Feed it `"oops"` and it would return an `Err`,
sending control to the other arm. The `Result` made the possibility of failure
impossible to overlook.

steps.title: Safe division
steps.intro:
You apply `Option` to make a dangerous operation safe. Integer division by zero
panics (crashes) in Rust. Instead of letting that happen, return an
`Option<i32>`: `None` when the divisor is zero, and `Some(a / b)` otherwise. The
caller is then forced to handle the "cannot divide" case — no crash, no silent
wrong answer.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `safe_div`:

```rust
pub fn safe_div(a: i32, b: i32) -> Option<i32> { ... }
```

Return `None` when `b` is `0`, otherwise `Some(a / b)`.

Examples:

- `safe_div(10, 2)` → `Some(5)`
- `safe_div(7, 0)` → `None`
- `safe_div(-9, 3)` → `Some(-3)`

**Hint:** guard the zero case first with an `if`, then return `Some(a / b)`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The function does one comparison and at most one division — the same work for any
input, with no loop and no allocation — so time and space are both constant:
**O(1)**. Returning `Option<i32>` turns a potential runtime panic (divide by zero)
into a value the caller must handle, which is the whole point of error handling in
Rust.

units.title: Database: connect & query
units.intro: Databases are how real programs remember things. In this track you drive SQLite directly from Rust with the `rusqlite` crate — no server to run, just a library. You start here by opening a database, creating a table, inserting rows with bound parameters, and reading results back as Rust values. By the end you let SQL count adults for you under hidden tests.

steps.title: Opening a database and running SQL
steps.intro: A database is just structured storage you talk to in SQL. The `rusqlite` crate gives you a `Connection` — a handle to one SQLite database — and lets you run statements and read rows back as ordinary Rust values. You bind inputs as parameters instead of pasting them into the SQL text, which is both safer and faster.

steps.title: Open, create, insert, count
steps.intro: The smallest useful database program: open an in-memory database, create a table, insert a row with a bound parameter, and count the rows.
steps.prompt:
Open an in-memory SQLite database, create a table, insert one row using a bound `?1` parameter, and read back the row count.

**Why:** every database interaction is this loop — connect, run SQL, read a result as a Rust value. Binding `?1` keeps values out of the SQL text, the habit that prevents injection.
line_comments: Brings `Connection`, rusqlite's handle to one database, into scope.
Opens a brand-new SQLite database that lives only in memory.
Runs a `CREATE TABLE` statement; `[]` means no bound parameters.
Inserts one row, binding the name to the `?1` placeholder (no string-building).
Begins a single-row read; `query_row` expects exactly one row.
The SQL counts the rows; the closure reads column 0 of the result.
Unwraps the `Result`, panicking only if the query failed.
Prints `rows = 1` — the one row we inserted.
steps.explanation: The program opened a private in-memory database, created a table, inserted one row (binding the city name to `?1`), and asked SQLite to count the rows — `rows = 1`. No file, no server: the database lived entirely in memory and disappeared when `main` returned.

steps.title: Read one value with a bound lookup
steps.intro: A `WHERE` clause with a bound parameter is how you fetch exactly the row you want. Here you store a product and read its price back by id.
steps.prompt:
Insert a product row, then read its price back with a `WHERE id = ?1` lookup.

**Why:** `query_row` is the one-row read, and binding the id as `?1` means the database — not string concatenation — decides what the value is.
line_comments: Opens an in-memory database to work in.
Begins a `CREATE TABLE` for a product with an id and a price...
Inserts a row, binding `1` to `?1` and `250` to `?2`...
Selects the price of the row whose id equals the bound `?1` (`1`).
steps.explanation: Binding `1` to `?1` in the `WHERE` clause fetched exactly one row, and `query_row` handed its `price` column to the closure — `price = 250`. The value travelled as a parameter, never as text spliced into the SQL.

steps.title: Iterate many rows with query_map
steps.intro: When a query returns many rows, `prepare` a statement once and `query_map` turns each row into a Rust value you can iterate.
steps.prompt:
Seed three numbers, then read them all back with a prepared statement and sum them.

**Why:** `query_row` is for one row; `prepare` + `query_map` is the pattern for many, giving you an iterator of typed results.
line_comments: Loops over three literal numbers to seed the table.
Prepares a reusable statement that selects every `v` in order.
`query_map` turns each row into an `i64`, yielding an iterator.
Sums the iterator after unwrapping each row.
steps.explanation: The prepared statement was run once and `query_map` yielded one `i64` per row; summing them gave `sum = 60`. Preparing the statement separates compiling the SQL from executing it, which is what you want when a query runs more than once.

steps.title: Count adults
steps.intro: You apply the open-insert-query loop end to end. Given a list of `(name, age)` pairs, insert them into a table and let SQL — not a Rust loop — count how many are adults (age 18 or older) with a `COUNT(*) ... WHERE` query.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `count_adults`:

```rust
pub fn count_adults(rows: &[(String, i64)]) -> i64 { ... }
```

Create an in-memory table, insert every `(name, age)` row with bound parameters, then return the result of `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ... WHERE age >= 18`.

Examples:

- `[]` → `0`
- `[("A", 20), ("B", 10), ("C", 40)]` → `2`
- `[("A", 18), ("B", 17)]` → `1` (18 counts)

**Hint:** open with `Connection::open_in_memory()`, insert in a loop with `params![name, age]`, and let the database do the counting.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification: Inserting the `n` rows is linear work, and the `COUNT(*) ... WHERE age >= 18` scans them once — so time is **O(n)**; the rows live in the table, so space is **O(n)** too. Pushing the count into SQL (a `WHERE` plus `COUNT`) rather than looping in Rust lets the database filter and tally in a single pass, which is the whole point of querying instead of fetching everything and counting by hand.

units.title: Database: transactions & atomicity
units.intro: A transaction is a group of changes that must all succeed together or all be undone — no middle ground. That is how a bank transfer never loses money to a crash halfway through. Here you commit, roll back, and lean on `rusqlite`'s automatic rollback-on-drop, then prove atomicity by moving money between two accounts under hidden tests.

steps.title: Transactions: all or nothing
steps.intro: Some changes must happen together or not at all — moving money out of one account and into another, for instance. A transaction groups statements so they either all commit or all roll back, never halfway. This 'all-or-nothing' guarantee is called atomicity, and it is the reason databases can be trusted with money.
steps.body:
## Atomicity with transactions

A transaction wraps several statements into one unit. Until you **commit**, the changes are pending; a **rollback** throws them all away. In `rusqlite` you start one with `Connection::transaction`, which borrows the connection mutably:

```rust
let tx = conn.transaction().unwrap();
tx.execute("UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1", []).unwrap();
tx.execute("UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2", []).unwrap();
tx.commit().unwrap(); // both updates become permanent together
```

If anything is wrong, you roll back instead, and the database is left exactly as it was:

```rust
tx.rollback().unwrap(); // neither update survives
```

There is a safety net: if a `Transaction` is dropped without `commit`, `rusqlite` **rolls it back automatically**. So an early return or a panic cannot leave a half-finished change behind — the default is to undo. That default is what makes transactions a guarantee rather than a hope.

steps.title: Commit a transaction
steps.intro: A committed transaction makes its changes permanent. Subtract from a balance inside a transaction, commit, and read the new value.
steps.prompt:
Open a transaction, update a balance, `commit`, and read it back.

**Why:** `commit` is the moment pending changes become real. Before it, nothing is visible outside the transaction; after it, the change is durable.
line_comments: Opens the database as `mut` — a transaction needs a mutable borrow.
Creates an `acct` table with a single balance column.
Seeds one account with a balance of 100.
Begins a transaction; changes now stay pending until committed.
Subtracts 40 from the balance inside the transaction.
`commit` makes the change permanent and ends the transaction.
Starts reading the balance back out.
steps.explanation: Inside the transaction the balance dropped from 100 to 60, and `commit` made that permanent — the read afterwards saw `bal = 60`. Commit is the dividing line between a provisional change and a durable one.

steps.title: Roll a transaction back
steps.intro: A rollback discards everything the transaction did. Make the same change as before, but roll back instead of committing, and watch it vanish.
steps.prompt:
Open a transaction, update a balance, `rollback`, and read it back unchanged.

**Why:** rollback is the escape hatch. When a step fails, rolling back restores the database to exactly where it started — the heart of atomicity.
line_comments: Opens the database as `mut` for the transaction.
Subtracts 40 — but only provisionally, inside the transaction.
steps.explanation: The subtraction happened inside the transaction, but `rollback` discarded it, so the balance read back as `bal = 100` — exactly its starting value. Nothing the transaction did survived, which is the guarantee you lean on when a step fails.

steps.title: An uncommitted transaction auto-rolls-back
steps.intro: `rusqlite` rolls a transaction back automatically if you drop it without committing. Change a balance inside a scope, leave without committing, and see the change undone.
steps.prompt:
Make a change inside an inner scope, never call `commit`, and read the balance back unchanged after the scope ends.

**Why:** the safe default is *undo*. A panic or early return drops the transaction, and the automatic rollback means a half-finished change can never leak out.
line_comments: Opens an inner scope to bound the transaction's lifetime.
Begins a transaction inside the scope.
Adds 500 provisionally — but we never call `commit`.
The scope ends, dropping `tx`; an uncommitted transaction auto-rolls-back.
Prints `bal = 100` — the dropped transaction left nothing behind.
steps.explanation: The `+ 500` update ran inside the transaction, but the inner scope ended without a `commit`, so dropping `tx` rolled it back — the balance stayed `bal = 100`. Because undo is the default, forgetting to commit fails safe instead of corrupting data.

steps.title: Atomic transfer
steps.intro: You prove atomicity with money. Two accounts start with balances `a0` and `b0`. In a single transaction, move `amount` from A to B. If that would push *either* balance below zero, roll the whole transaction back and return the original balances unchanged. Otherwise commit and return the new balances.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `transfer`:

```rust
pub fn transfer(a0: i64, b0: i64, amount: i64) -> (i64, i64) { ... }
```

Seed two accounts, open one transaction, debit A and credit B, then check: if either balance is now negative, `rollback` and return `(a0, b0)`; otherwise `commit` and return the new `(a, b)`.

Examples:

- `transfer(100, 0, 30)` → `(70, 30)` (commits)
- `transfer(50, 0, 80)` → `(50, 0)` (A would go negative → rolls back)
- `transfer(100, 0, -10)` → `(100, 0)` (B would go negative → rolls back)
- `transfer(100, 0, 100)` → `(0, 100)` (exact, still valid)

**Hint:** open the database as `mut`, do both `UPDATE`s inside `conn.transaction()`, read the two balances, then `rollback` or `commit` based on the sign.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification: The work is a fixed handful of statements regardless of the numbers — two updates, two reads, and one commit-or-rollback — so time and space are both **O(1)**. The transaction is what makes the result trustworthy: debit and credit either both land or both vanish, so the two accounts can never be seen in a half-moved state, and a would-be-negative balance leaves the books exactly as they started.

units.title: Database: WAL & connection pools
units.intro: Real services hit one database from many threads at once. This unit shows the two tools that make that safe and fast: WAL mode, which lets readers run while a writer writes, and a connection pool (`r2d2` + `r2d2_sqlite`) that lends each thread its own connection. You finish by making several threads cooperate on a shared database and produce the same total every time, under hidden tests.

steps.title: Concurrency: WAL and connection pools
steps.intro: When several threads touch one database, two things help. WAL mode (write-ahead logging) lets readers keep reading while a writer writes, instead of everyone blocking. A connection pool hands each thread its own connection from a managed set, so you neither open a new one every time nor share one unsafely. Writes still serialize — SQLite allows one writer at a time — but the result stays correct and, when the work is commutative, deterministic.

steps.title: Turn on WAL mode
steps.intro: WAL mode needs a real file. Open a file-backed database and switch its journal mode to WAL, reading back the mode SQLite confirms.
steps.prompt:
Open a file-backed SQLite database and set `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`, printing the mode it reports.

**Why:** WAL is the setting that lets readers and a writer work at once. It only applies to on-disk databases, so the program writes to a temp file.
line_comments: Builds a path to a database file in the system temp directory.
Removes any leftover file so we start from a clean database.
Opens (creating) that on-disk database — WAL needs a real file, not memory.
Starts reading the result of the pragma.
Sets the journal mode to WAL and reads back the mode SQLite chose.
Prints `mode = wal` — write-ahead logging is now on.
steps.explanation: Setting `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` on the file-backed database returned `wal`, so readers can now proceed alongside a writer. The same pragma on an in-memory database would report `memory` instead — WAL is a property of a real file.

steps.title: Check a connection out of a pool
steps.intro: A pool lends you a connection and takes it back when you are done. Build a small pool and run a trivial query through a borrowed connection.
steps.prompt:
Build an `r2d2` pool over `r2d2_sqlite`, check out one connection, and run `SELECT 1`.

**Why:** pooling is how you share a database across many tasks without opening a fresh connection each time or unsafely sharing one.
line_comments: Brings the pooled connection manager from `r2d2_sqlite` into scope.
Creates a manager that hands out in-memory SQLite connections.
Builds an r2d2 pool holding up to four live connections.
Checks one connection out of the pool.
Closes `main`; the connection returns to the pool when dropped.
steps.explanation: The pool built four connections up front and lent one out for `pool.get()`; `SELECT 1` ran on it and returned `one = 1`. When the borrowed connection is dropped it goes back to the pool, ready for the next caller — no per-task open.

steps.title: Pooled writes from four threads
steps.intro: Each thread borrows its own pooled connection and inserts one value into a shared file-backed database. Because addition is commutative and writes serialize, the final sum is always the same.
steps.prompt:
Share a pool across four threads, each inserting one number into a shared database, then read the total.

**Why:** this is the shape of real concurrent database work — a pool per worker, serialized writes, and a result that does not depend on thread order.
line_comments: Brings the pooled connection manager into scope.
Brings `thread` in so we can spawn workers.
Builds a temp-file path so every pooled connection shares one database.
...initialising each connection with a busy timeout so writers wait, not fail.
Builds a four-connection pool over that manager.
Checks out one connection to create the shared table.
Prepares a vector to hold the worker handles.
Loops over four values, one per worker.
Clones the pool handle (a cheap `Arc`) to move into the thread.
Each worker checks out its own pooled connection.
...and inserts its one value; SQLite serializes the writes.
Closes the thread closure and stores the handle.
...so `main` waits for all inserts to finish.
Checks out a connection for the final read.
Sums all inserted values with `SELECT SUM(v)`.
Prints `sum = 10` — the same result whichever thread ran first.
steps.explanation: Four threads each borrowed a pooled connection and inserted one value; the writes took turns (SQLite allows one writer at a time), and summing afterwards gave `sum = 10` — 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. The order the threads ran in never mattered, because addition is commutative and every write landed before the final read.

steps.title: Deterministic pooled sum
steps.intro: You make concurrency produce a guaranteed answer. Using a WAL, file-backed, pooled SQLite database, spawn `workers` threads. Each thread inserts a disjoint slice of the numbers `1..=upto`, then after all threads finish you read `SELECT SUM(x)`. The result must always equal `upto*(upto+1)/2`, no matter how the threads interleave.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `pooled_sum`:

```rust
pub fn pooled_sum(upto: i64, workers: usize) -> i64 { ... }
```

Build a pool over a file-backed SQLite database with WAL on and a busy timeout. Partition `1..=upto` into `workers` disjoint slices (for example, worker `w` takes every number congruent to `w` modulo `workers`), insert each slice from its own thread, join, then return `SELECT SUM(x)`.

Examples:

- `pooled_sum(100, 4)` → `5050`
- `pooled_sum(1000, 8)` → `500500`
- `pooled_sum(0, 4)` → `0`
- `pooled_sum(10, 1)` → `55`

**Hint:** give each new connection `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000;` via `with_init`, use a unique temp-file path per call, clone the pool into each thread, and `join` them all before reading the sum.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification: Every number from 1 to `upto` is inserted exactly once across the threads, so the total work and the stored rows are both linear — time and space **O(n)**. The determinism comes from the design, not luck: the slices are disjoint (each number written once), WAL plus a busy timeout make concurrent writers wait rather than fail, and the sum is read only after every thread is joined — so the answer is always `upto*(upto+1)/2` regardless of interleaving.

units.title: Database: the N+1 problem
units.intro: One of the most common database performance bugs is quietly running a query inside a loop — one query to get a list, then N more, one per item. This unit makes the cost visible by counting queries, then fixes it with a single `IN (...)` or `JOIN`. You finish by computing a total with exactly one query and proving the count, under hidden tests.

steps.title: The N+1 query problem
steps.intro: A classic performance bug: you fetch a list, then loop and run one more query per item. One query plus N queries — the 'N+1' problem. Each round-trip to the database has a cost, and N of them in a loop is slow. The fix is to ask for everything you need in a single query, with `IN (...)` or a `JOIN`.
steps.body:
## One query in a loop is N queries

Here is the trap. You have some ids and fetch each row separately:

```rust
let mut total = 0;
for id in &ids {
    let price: i64 = conn
        .query_row("SELECT price FROM p WHERE id = ?1", [id], |r| r.get(0))
        .unwrap();
    total += price; // one database round-trip per id
}
```

With 1000 ids that is 1000 queries. The database spends most of its time on round-trip overhead, not on the actual work.

## Ask once

Fetch the whole set in a single query with `IN (...)` — or a `JOIN` when the data spans tables:

```rust
let total: i64 = conn
    .query_row("SELECT SUM(price) FROM p WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3)", [], |r| r.get(0))
    .unwrap();
```

Same answer, one round-trip. The rule of thumb: if you find yourself running queries inside a loop, step back and ask whether one `IN` or `JOIN` could do the whole job at once. Almost always, it can.

steps.title: The N+1 loop (one query per id)
steps.intro: This is the anti-pattern itself: loop over ids and run a separate query for each, counting how many queries that costs.
steps.prompt:
Loop over three ids, run one `SELECT` per id, and count the queries.

**Why:** seeing the counter reach 3 for 3 ids makes the cost concrete — N ids mean N round-trips, and this scales badly.
line_comments: Creates a `p` table with id and price.
Inserts each row, binding id and price.
Counts how many SQL queries we run.
Loops once per id — this is the N+1 shape.
Counts this query — one per iteration.
Adds the fetched price to the total.
Closes the loop — three ids meant three queries.
steps.explanation: Three ids drove three separate `SELECT`s — `queries = 3` — to reach `total = 60`. The counter is the point: the number of round-trips grows with the number of ids, which is exactly why this pattern gets slow.

steps.title: Fix it with one IN query
steps.intro: The same result in a single query. Replace the loop with one `SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...)` and watch the query count drop to one.
steps.prompt:
Fetch the sum of three prices with a single `IN` query, and report one query.

**Why:** `IN (...)` collapses N lookups into one round-trip — identical answer, a fraction of the cost.
line_comments: Begins a single read for the whole set.
One query sums the prices for all ids via `IN (...)`.
Exactly one query ran this time.
Prints `total = 60 queries = 1` — same answer, one round-trip.
steps.explanation: One `SELECT ... WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3)` produced `total = 60` with `queries = 1` — the same result the N+1 loop computed, but in a single round-trip. That is the whole fix: fold the loop into one query.

steps.title: Combine tables with one JOIN
steps.intro: When the data you need spans two tables, a `JOIN` fetches it in one query instead of looking up each related row separately.
steps.prompt:
Join an `ord` table to a `prod` table and sum each order's product price in a single query.

**Why:** a `JOIN` is the cross-table version of the same lesson — relate rows inside the database, in one query, rather than looping in Rust.
line_comments: Creates an `ord` table linking each order to a product id.
Creates a `prod` table with product prices.
Seeds three orders pointing at those products.
Begins a single read for the grand total.
Opens the `query_row` call across several lines.
One JOIN sums each order's product price in a single query.
No bound parameters for this query.
steps.explanation: The `JOIN` matched each order to its product and summed the prices in one query — `total = 250` from orders pointing at products priced 100, 50, and 100. Without the join you would have looked up each order's product separately: the N+1 trap again, now across tables.

steps.title: Beat N+1 with one query
steps.intro: You prove you can avoid the N+1 trap. Given a slice of `order_ids`, return a pair: the total price of those orders, and the number of SQL queries you ran to get it. Using a single `IN (...)` query, that number must be exactly 1 — not N. An empty slice needs no query at all.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `total_price`:

```rust
pub fn total_price(order_ids: &[i64]) -> (i64, usize) { ... }
```

Seed a deterministic `orders` table (order `i` has price `i * 10`, for `i` in `1..=100`). For a non-empty `order_ids`, build one `SELECT SUM(price) ... WHERE id IN (...)` query, run it once, and return `(sum, 1)`. For an empty slice, return `(0, 0)` without querying.

Examples:

- `total_price(&[1, 2, 3])` → `(60, 1)`
- `total_price(&[])` → `(0, 0)`
- `total_price(&[999])` → `(0, 1)` (no such order, still one query)
- `total_price(&[100])` → `(1000, 1)`

**Hint:** build the `IN (?, ?, ...)` placeholders from the slice length and pass the ids with `rusqlite::params_from_iter`; wrap the sum in `COALESCE(SUM(price), 0)` so a no-match returns `0`, not `NULL`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification: Building the `IN` clause and binding the ids is linear in `k`, the number of ids, and the database answers in a single query — so time and space are **O(k)** in the input, with exactly one round-trip. Returning the query count alongside the sum is the proof: whether you ask for one order or fifty, the count stays 1, because `IN (...)` does in one statement what the naive loop would do in N.

units.title: Database: pagination done right
units.intro: Showing results a page at a time sounds trivial, but the obvious `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` approach slows down on deep pages and can skip or duplicate rows when data shifts. This unit contrasts it with keyset (seek) pagination — `WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ?` — which stays fast and stable. You finish by implementing keyset paging over a seeded table, under hidden tests.

steps.title: Pagination: offset vs keyset
steps.intro: You rarely want every row at once — you want a page of them. The familiar way is `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`, but it gets slower the deeper you go and can skip or repeat rows when data changes underneath you. Keyset (or 'seek') pagination remembers the last id you saw and asks for rows *after* it, which stays fast and stable.
steps.body:
## LIMIT / OFFSET

The textbook page: skip `OFFSET` rows, take `LIMIT`:

```rust
// page 3 of size 10: skip 20, take 10
let sql = "SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20";
```

It works, but the database must still walk and discard all `OFFSET` rows, so page 10000 is slow. Worse, if rows are inserted or deleted between pages, the offset shifts and you can skip or repeat items.

## Keyset / seek pagination

Instead of counting from the start, remember the last id and seek past it:

```rust
let sql = "SELECT id FROM t WHERE id > ?1 ORDER BY id LIMIT ?2";
// pass (last_id_seen, page_size)
```

The `WHERE id > ?1` jumps straight to where you left off using the primary-key order, so every page costs the same no matter how deep. Because the cursor is a real id rather than a position, inserts and deletes elsewhere cannot make you skip or repeat a row. The one rule: order by a stable, unique column (an id is ideal).

steps.title: Page with LIMIT and OFFSET
steps.intro: The classic page: skip some rows, take a few. Read the second page of three from a table of ten ids.
steps.prompt:
Select a page with `ORDER BY id LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3`.

**Why:** `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` is the familiar way to page, and it is fine for shallow pages — but the database must skip every offset row to get there.
line_comments: Creates a `t` table keyed by id.
Collects the page into a vector...
Prints `page = [4, 5, 6]` — the second page of three.
steps.explanation: `OFFSET 3 LIMIT 3` over the ordered ids skipped 1, 2, 3 and returned `page = [4, 5, 6]`. It is simple and correct here, but to reach that page the database still had to walk past the three skipped rows — a cost that grows with the offset.

steps.title: Seek past the last id
steps.intro: Keyset pagination asks for rows *after* a remembered id. Fetch the next three ids after id 6.
steps.prompt:
Select the next page with `WHERE id > ?1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3`.

**Why:** seeking past a known id jumps straight to the next page using the key order, so the cost does not grow with depth and the page stays stable.
line_comments: Remembers the last id seen on the previous page.
...take the next 3 rows strictly after `?1`, ordered by id.
steps.explanation: `WHERE id > 6 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3` sought straight past id 6 and returned `page = [7, 8, 9]`. No rows were skipped and discarded: the index on `id` jumped to the cursor, which is why keyset paging keeps the same cost on page 2 or page 2,000,000.

steps.title: Walk pages by advancing a cursor
steps.intro: Keyset paging chains: each page's last id becomes the next page's cursor. Advance a size-one cursor twice and see where it lands.
steps.prompt:
Advance a cursor through two single-row pages, each time seeking the next id after the cursor.

**Why:** the cursor *is* the state between pages. Feeding the last id back in is how you walk a whole table one page at a time.
line_comments: Starts the cursor before the first id.
Advances the cursor twice, one page of size 1 each time.
Begins reading the next id after the cursor...
Moves the cursor forward to the id we just read.
Prints `cursor = 2` — two single-row pages advanced 0 to 1 to 2.
steps.explanation: Starting at cursor 0, each step fetched the smallest id greater than the cursor and moved it forward: 0 to 1, then 1 to 2 — `cursor = 2`. Chaining the last id into the next query is the whole mechanism behind walking a table with keyset pagination.

steps.title: Keyset pagination
steps.intro: You implement stable, efficient paging. Over a seeded table of ids `1..=100`, return the next `size` ids strictly after `last_id`, in ascending order. This is keyset pagination: a `WHERE id > ?` seek with a `LIMIT`, not an `OFFSET` count.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `page_after`:

```rust
pub fn page_after(last_id: i64, size: i64) -> Vec<i64> { ... }
```

Seed a table with ids `1..=100`, then return the ids `x` with `x > last_id`, ordered ascending, at most `size` of them. A `size` of zero or less returns an empty vector.

Examples:

- `page_after(0, 5)` → `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`
- `page_after(5, 3)` → `[6, 7, 8]`
- `page_after(98, 5)` → `[99, 100]` (only two left)
- `page_after(100, 5)` → `[]` (nothing after the last id)

**Hint:** one prepared statement — `SELECT id FROM items WHERE id > ?1 ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT ?2` — binding `(last_id, size)` and collecting the rows.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification: The seek uses the primary-key order to jump straight to the first id after `last_id`, then reads at most `size` rows — so the time and the returned vector are both **O(size)**, independent of how deep into the table the page sits. That is the advantage over `OFFSET`, which would have to walk and discard every row before the page; the `WHERE id > ?` cursor also keeps the page stable when other rows change.

units.title: Database: indexes & query plans
units.intro: An index is what separates an instant lookup from a slow full-table scan. This unit shows how to create one and — crucially — how to confirm it is used, with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`, which reports `SEARCH ... USING INDEX` versus `SCAN`. You finish by writing code that inspects the plan and proves the index is doing its job, under hidden tests.

steps.title: Indexes and query plans
steps.intro: Without an index, finding rows by a column means scanning the whole table — fine for ten rows, ruinous for ten million. An index is a sorted structure the database can search quickly, turning a full scan into a direct lookup. You do not have to guess whether it is used: `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` tells you exactly how SQLite will run a query.
steps.body:
## Indexes

A lookup on an unindexed column forces a full-table **scan**. Create an index and the database can **search** straight to the matching rows:

```rust
conn.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email)", []).unwrap();
```

## EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN

To see whether an index is actually used, prefix a query with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`. It returns rows describing the strategy; the useful part is the detail text in column 3:

```rust
let plan: String = conn
    .query_row(
        "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM users WHERE email = ?1",
        ["a@b.c"],
        |r| r.get(3),
    )
    .unwrap();
```

With the index you will see a detail like `SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_users_email (email=?)`; without it, `SCAN users`. The word **SEARCH** with `USING INDEX` means a fast, targeted lookup; **SCAN** means reading every row. Reading the plan is how you confirm an index is doing its job rather than assuming it is.

steps.title: EXPLAIN shows the index is used
steps.intro: Create an index, then ask SQLite how it would run a lookup on the indexed column. The plan says it uses the index.
steps.prompt:
Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for a `WHERE email = ?` lookup on an indexed column and check the plan contains `USING INDEX`.

**Why:** the query plan is ground truth. Instead of hoping the index helps, you read SQLite's own description of the strategy.
line_comments: Creates a `u` table with an email column and an extra `name` column.
Creates an index on the `email` column.
...for an `email =` lookup that selects `name`, so it is not index-covering.
Reads the plan's detail text from column 3.
steps.explanation: The plan for the indexed `email =` lookup read `SEARCH ... USING INDEX idx_email`, so the check printed `true`. Selecting `name` (a non-indexed column) keeps it a plain index search rather than a covering one, and either way the index is doing the finding.

steps.title: Without an index it scans
