steps.intro: The same query with no index gets a very different plan. See SQLite fall back to scanning every row.
steps.prompt:
Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for the same lookup on an *unindexed* column and check the plan says `SCAN`.

**Why:** contrast makes the lesson stick. No index means a full-table scan — exactly what the plan reports.
line_comments: Creates a `u` table with NO index this time.
Begins preparing the same `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`...
...for an `email =` lookup with nothing to help it.
Reads the plan's detail text from column 3.
Prints `true` — the detail says `SCAN`, a full-table scan.
steps.explanation: With no index on `email`, the plan read `SCAN u` and the check printed `true` — SQLite would examine every row to answer the lookup. Compared with the previous drill's `USING INDEX`, this is the difference an index makes, straight from the query plan.

steps.title: An indexed lookup returns the row
steps.intro: Beyond the plan, the index just makes lookups work well. Seed a hundred rows with an index and fetch one by email.
steps.prompt:
Create an index, seed a hundred rows, and fetch one id by its email.

**Why:** the payoff of an index is this everyday lookup — finding one row among many by a searchable column, quickly and correctly.
line_comments: Creates a `u` table with id and email.
Creates an index on `email` to speed lookups.
Loops to seed one hundred rows.
Builds a distinct email for each row.
Begins the indexed lookup for one email.
Selects the id whose email matches the bound value.
Prints `id = 42` — the row we searched for.
steps.explanation: With an index on `email`, the `WHERE email = 'user42@x.io'` lookup went straight to the matching row and returned `id = 42`. Across a hundred rows the difference is invisible, but the same targeted search is what keeps a lookup instant across millions.

steps.title: Confirm the index is used
steps.intro: You verify an optimization instead of assuming it. Create a table and an index on a column, then run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for a `WHERE indexed_col = ?` lookup and return `true` only if the plan actually uses the index — that is, its detail text contains `USING INDEX`.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement `uses_index_for_lookup`:

```rust
pub fn uses_index_for_lookup() -> bool { ... }
```

Create a table with an indexed column (and at least one non-indexed column so the plan is a plain index search, not a covering one), add the index, then run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for a `WHERE <indexed_col> = ?` query. Collect the plan's detail text and return whether it contains the substring `USING INDEX`.

Examples:

- With an index on the looked-up column → `true`
- The result is deterministic: calling it twice gives the same answer

**Hint:** the plan detail is column index 3 of each `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` row; join the rows' details and test with `.contains("USING INDEX")`. Select a non-indexed column in the query so SQLite reports `USING INDEX` rather than `USING COVERING INDEX`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification: The function builds a tiny fixed table, adds one index, and inspects a single query plan — a constant amount of work, so time and space are **O(1)**. The value is methodological: rather than trusting that an index helps, it reads SQLite's own `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` and confirms the lookup resolves via `USING INDEX` (a targeted search) instead of a full-table `SCAN`, which is how you verify a performance assumption instead of guessing.

units.title: Traits & impl: behaviour as a contract
units.intro:
A trait is a named set of methods a type promises to provide — an interface, in
the vocabulary of other languages. You declare the contract once with `trait`,
then `impl` it for each concrete type. Code can then speak to "anything that
behaves like this" instead of to one specific type. By the end you implement a
trait and let a function greet any type that satisfies it.

steps.title: Shared behaviour, named once
steps.intro:
Programs repeat behaviour across unrelated types: many things can be "printed",
"compared", or "drawn". A trait captures that behaviour as a contract: a set of
method signatures a type agrees to supply. This is how Rust achieves
polymorphism without inheritance — types stay independent, and the shared
vocabulary lives in the trait.

steps.title: Define a trait and implement it
steps.intro:
The smallest useful trait: one method. You declare the contract, implement it
for a concrete type, then call the method through a value of that type. This is
the shape every later idea builds on.
steps.prompt:
Declare a trait with one method, implement it for a struct, and call it.

**Why:** a trait names behaviour; an `impl` block supplies it for one type. This
separation is what lets different types share a vocabulary.
line_comments: The one method every `Animal` must provide, taking `&self`.
A unit struct `Dog` with no fields.
Calls the trait method and prints `Woof`.
steps.explanation:
`Dog` now satisfies the `Animal` contract, so `d.speak()` resolves to the method
in the `impl` block and prints `Woof`. The trait and the type are declared
separately — exactly what lets many unrelated types share one named behaviour.

steps.title: A default method on a trait
steps.intro:
A trait method can ship with a body. Implementers that are happy with it write
nothing; the default is built from the *required* methods. Here `greet` is free
once you supply `name`.
steps.prompt:
Give the trait a default method that calls a required one.

**Why:** default methods let a trait provide behaviour in terms of a small set of
required methods, so implementers write less and stay consistent.
line_comments: A required method: the implementer must supply `name`.
A default method with a body...
Closes the `impl` (note: no `greet` written — the default is used).
Calls the inherited default `greet`, printing `Hello, Bot!`.
steps.explanation:
`Bot` only implemented `name`, yet `b.greet()` worked: it ran the trait's default
body, which called back into `self.name()`. Default methods let a trait give you
behaviour for free, expressed in terms of the few methods you must provide.

steps.title: One trait, two types
steps.intro:
The payoff of a trait is many implementers. Here two unrelated structs implement
the same trait, each in its own way, and the caller uses the same method name on
both. This is polymorphism without any inheritance.
steps.prompt:
Implement one trait for two different structs and call it on each.

**Why:** a trait lets unrelated types share a method name while each supplies its
own behaviour — the essence of Rust polymorphism.
line_comments: Same method name on `Cat` → `a cat purrs`.
Same method name on `Fish` → `a fish swims`.
steps.explanation:
Both `Cat` and `Fish` answer to `describe()`, yet neither knows about the other —
each `impl` block supplies its own body. The caller used one method name for two
types. That is how traits give you polymorphism without a class hierarchy.

steps.title: Greet through a trait
steps.intro:
You apply traits end to end. Define a `Greet` trait with a `hello` method, a
`Person` struct that implements it, and a function `greeting` that builds a
`Person` and returns its greeting. The hidden tests only see the final string,
but the clean way to produce it is through the trait.

gabarito.justification:
Building the greeting copies the name once and formats a new string, so both time
and space are linear in the name's length, **O(n)**. The point is the shape, not
the cost: behaviour lives in the `Greet` trait, `Person` implements it, and
`greeting` speaks only through the trait method `hello`.

units.title: Generics: write it once, for every type
units.intro:
A generic is code parameterised by a type you fill in later: `Vec<T>` works for
any `T`, and so can your own functions and structs. The compiler stamps out a
specialised copy for each concrete type you use (monomorphization), so generics
cost nothing at runtime. By the end you write one `max_of` that finds the largest
element of a slice of *any* comparable, copyable type.

steps.title: Type parameters
steps.intro:
Copy-pasting the same function for `i32`, then `f64`, then `String` is how bugs
and boredom breed. Generics let you write the logic once with a *type parameter*
— a stand-in like `T` — and the compiler generates a concrete version for each
type actually used. The abstraction is free: monomorphization means no runtime
tax.
steps.body:
## Type parameters with `<T>`

A **generic function** names one or more type parameters in angle brackets:

```rust
fn first<T: Copy>(xs: &[T]) -> T {
    xs[0]
}
```

`T` is a placeholder; call `first(&[1, 2, 3])` and `T` becomes `i32`.

A **generic struct** parameterises its fields:

```rust
struct Pair<T> {
    a: T,
    b: T,
}
```

The bound `T: Copy` after the parameter is a **constraint** — it says "whatever
`T` is, it must be copyable", which is what lets the body use the value. (Unit 12
digs into bounds.)

At compile time Rust performs **monomorphization**: for each concrete type you
use, it generates a specialised copy of the code. Generics are therefore as fast
as hand-written type-specific code — zero-cost abstraction.

steps.title: A generic function
steps.intro:
One function, two element types. `first` takes a slice of any `Copy` type and
returns its first element. The same code serves integers and string slices — the
compiler specialises it for each.
steps.prompt:
Write a generic `first<T: Copy>` and call it with two different slice types.

**Why:** a type parameter lets one function serve many types. `Copy` lets the
body return the element by value.
line_comments: Declares `first` with a type parameter `T` bounded by `Copy`.
Returns the first element by value (allowed because `T: Copy`).
An array of `i32` — here `T` will be `i32`.
An array of `&str` — here `T` will be `&str`.
Calls the SAME `first` on the strings; prints `a`.
steps.explanation:
One definition of `first` served both a slice of `i32` and a slice of `&str`. The
compiler monomorphized it into two specialised copies, so the call sites pay no
runtime cost. That is the deal generics offer: write once, specialise everywhere.

steps.title: A generic struct
steps.intro:
Data can be generic too. `Pair<T>` holds two values of the same type, and an
`impl` block bounded by `Display` gives it a method to show them. One struct, any
printable element type.
steps.prompt:
Define `Pair<T>` and give it a method via a bounded `impl` block.

**Why:** generic structs store any type; a bounded `impl` adds methods that need
a capability (here, being printable).
steps.explanation:
`Pair<T>` stored integers in `p` and string slices in `q`, and the same `show`
method printed both — because the `impl` block required `T: Display`, which both
`i32` and `&str` satisfy. Generic data plus a bounded `impl` is a common, powerful
combination.

steps.title: Generics with a bound
steps.intro:
A generic value is opaque until you say what it can do. `tag` accepts any
`Display` value and formats a `label=value` string. The bound is what unlocks the
`{value}` interpolation.
steps.prompt:
Write `tag<T: Display>` and format a key/value pair for two types.

**Why:** without a bound the body cannot do anything with `T`. `Display` lets you
interpolate it into a string.
line_comments: Declares `tag` with `T: Display`, taking a label and a value.
steps.explanation:
`tag` interpolated `value` into a string only because the bound `T: Display`
promised every `T` can be displayed. Called with an `i32` and a `&str`, the
compiler produced two specialised copies, each printing its `label=value`.

steps.title: Generic maximum
steps.intro:
You write genuinely generic code. Implement `max_of` that returns the largest
element of a slice, or `None` when the slice is empty — for *any* type that can be
compared and copied. The same function must work for integers, floats and
characters, which is the whole point of a type parameter with bounds.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement a generic maximum:

```rust
pub fn max_of<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(xs: &[T]) -> Option<T> { ... }
```

Return `None` for an empty slice, otherwise `Some(largest)`.

Examples:

- `max_of(&[3, 7, 2, 9, 4])` → `Some(9)`
- `max_of(&['a', 'z', 'm'])` → `Some('z')`
- `max_of::<i32>(&[])` → `None`

**Hint:** start from the first element with `xs.first()?`, then scan the rest
keeping the larger one.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
A single pass compares each of the `n` elements once, so time is **O(n)**; only
one `best` value is kept, so extra space is **O(1)**. The bounds earn their keep:
`PartialOrd` enables `x > best`, `Copy` lets `best` hold a value rather than a
borrow, and `xs.first()?` returns `None` for the empty slice. One definition
serves `i32`, `f64` and `char` alike.

units.title: Trait bounds: spelling out what a type can do
units.intro:
A bound is a requirement attached to a type parameter: `T: Display` means "any
`T`, as long as it can be displayed". You can write bounds inline (`<T: Display>`)
or, when they pile up, in a readable `where` clause. Bounds are checked at the
call site, so a generic that compiles is correct for every type that meets its
bounds. By the end you count matching elements of any comparable type.

steps.title: Bounds and the where clause
steps.intro:
Generics are powerful precisely because they are constrained. A bound is a
promise the caller must keep and the body may rely on. Rust checks it where the
generic is *used*, so the error points at the real mistake — unlike templates
that explode deep inside a library. The `where` clause is just a tidier place to
write bounds when they grow.
steps.body:
## Bounds: inline and `where`

A bound after a type parameter says what the type must provide:

```rust
fn show_all<T: std::fmt::Debug>(xs: &[T]) { /* can use {:?} on each */ }
```

Several bounds combine with `+`:

```rust
fn twice<T: std::fmt::Display + Clone>(x: T) -> String { /* ... */ }
```

When the list grows, a **`where` clause** keeps the signature readable:

```rust
fn join<T>(xs: &[T], sep: &str) -> String
where
    T: std::fmt::Display,
{
    /* ... */
}
```

Inline and `where` mean exactly the same thing. Either way, the compiler verifies
at the call site that your concrete type satisfies the bound — so a generic that
type-checks works for *every* type allowed to call it.

steps.title: An inline bound
steps.intro:
The simplest bound sits right after the type parameter. `show_all` needs each
element to be `Debug` so it can print it with `{:?}`. Try to use `T` without the
bound and the compiler stops you — that is bounds doing their job.
steps.prompt:
Write `show_all<T: Debug>` that prints each element of a slice.

**Why:** the body can only use a capability it has asked for. `T: Debug` unlocks
`{:?}`.
line_comments: Declares `show_all` with the inline bound `T: Debug`.
Prints each element with `{:?}`, legal because of the bound.
Calls `show_all` on a slice of `i32`; prints `1`, `2`, `3` on three lines.
steps.explanation:
`show_all` printed every element because the bound `T: Debug` promised each one
could be formatted with `{:?}`. Remove the bound and the `println!` would not
compile — the body may only use capabilities it has declared.

steps.title: The where clause
steps.intro:
When a signature gets busy, move the bounds into a `where` clause below it. It
reads the same to the compiler but far better to a human. Here `join` turns any
slice of `Display` values into one separated string.
steps.prompt:
Rewrite a bound as a `where` clause on a `join` function.

**Why:** `where` keeps the function header clean when bounds multiply, with no
change in meaning.
line_comments: ...`T: Display`, so each element can become a string.
Maps each element to its `String` form and collects them.
Joins the parts with the separator.
steps.explanation:
The `where` clause moved the `T: Display` bound out of the header, leaving
`join<T>` easy to read — and the compiler treats it identically to an inline
bound. `join` then worked for ints and strings alike, producing `1-2-3` and
`a, b`.

steps.title: Several bounds with +
steps.intro:
A type parameter can be asked for more than one capability at once, joined with
`+`. `twice` needs `Clone` to duplicate the value and `Display` to print both
copies. Each bound unlocks exactly one thing the body does.
steps.prompt:
Require `Display + Clone` on one type parameter and use both.

**Why:** real functions often need several capabilities; `+` composes bounds, and
each one justifies a line of the body.
line_comments: Declares `twice<T>` taking the value by value.
`clone()` is legal because of the `Clone` bound.
`{a}` and `{x}` are legal because of the `Display` bound.
steps.explanation:
`twice` leaned on two bounds at once: `Clone` to duplicate `x` and `Display` to
print both copies. Joining them with `+` is how one type parameter can be asked
for several capabilities — each bound paying for one thing the body does.

steps.title: Count the matches
steps.intro:
You put a `where` clause to work. Implement `count_matching`, which counts how
many elements of a slice equal a given target — for any type that supports
equality. The single bound `T: PartialEq` is what lets the body compare elements,
and it is the only thing the function needs to know about `T`.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Count equal elements, generically:

```rust
pub fn count_matching<T>(xs: &[T], target: &T) -> usize
where
    T: PartialEq,
{ ... }
```

Return how many elements of `xs` are equal to `target`.

Examples:

- `count_matching(&[1, 2, 2, 3, 2], &2)` → `3`
- `count_matching(&["a", "b", "a"], &"a")` → `2`
- `count_matching(&[1, 2, 3], &9)` → `0`

**Hint:** iterate and `filter` on equality, then `count`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
One pass visits each of the `n` elements once and keeps only a running count, so
time is **O(n)** and extra space is **O(1)**. The `where T: PartialEq` bound is the
whole contract: it is exactly what makes `x == target` legal, and nothing else
about `T` matters, so the function serves ints, `&str`, and anything else
comparable.

units.title: Associated types: a type the trait names
units.intro:
Some traits need to name a related type, not just methods. `Iterator` declares
`type Item` — the kind of value it yields — and every implementer pins it down.
Associated types keep signatures clean: you write `fn next(&mut self) ->
Option<Self::Item>` once instead of threading an extra generic everywhere. By the
end you implement `Iterator` for your own type and generate a Fibonacci sequence.

steps.title: Types that belong to a trait
steps.intro:
A generic parameter lets the *caller* choose a type; an associated type lets the
*implementer* fix one. When each implementing type has exactly one natural choice
— an iterator yields one kind of item — an associated type expresses that better
than a generic, and keeps every downstream signature free of extra parameters.

steps.title: Implement Iterator
steps.intro:
Make your own type iterable by implementing `Iterator`: choose `type Item` and
write `next`. A `Countdown` yields numbers down to 1, then stops by returning
`None`. Once `next` exists, a `for` loop just works.
steps.prompt:
Implement `Iterator` for a `Countdown`, setting `type Item` and writing `next`.

**Why:** `Iterator` is defined with an associated `Item`. Supplying it and `next`
is all a `for` loop needs.
line_comments: A struct holding the current counter.
Pins the associated type: this iterator yields `u32`.
Otherwise there is still a value...
...and yield what it was before the step.
A `for` loop drives `next` until it returns `None`.
steps.explanation:
By choosing `type Item = u32` and writing `next`, `Countdown` became a real
iterator, so the `for` loop drove it to print `3`, `2`, `1` and stopped when
`next` returned `None`. The associated type is what told the loop each value is a
`u32`.

steps.title: Your own associated type
steps.intro:
Associated types are not just for `Iterator`. Define a `Container` trait with
`type Item`, and each implementer decides what it contains. Here `Bytes` sets
`Item = u8`, so `get` returns a byte.
steps.prompt:
Declare a trait with an associated type and implement it.

**Why:** when each type has one natural element type, an associated type states
it directly, keeping method signatures free of extra generics.
line_comments: Its associated type — chosen by each implementer.
A method whose return type is the associated `Self::Item`.
A struct wrapping a vector of bytes.
steps.explanation:
`Bytes` set `type Item = u8`, so `get` was free to return a plain `u8` and the
caller got `20`. The associated type let the trait name a related type once,
instead of forcing every method and caller to carry an extra generic parameter.

steps.title: The payoff: adaptors for free
steps.intro:
Because `Iterator` is one trait with an associated `Item`, the standard library
can build dozens of adaptors on top of `next` alone — `filter`, `map`, `sum`,
`collect`. You implement nothing here; you simply reap what the associated type
makes possible.
steps.prompt:
Use standard iterator adaptors that rely on the associated `Item` type.

**Why:** `sum`, `filter`, `collect` are defined once over any `Iterator`,
regardless of its `Item` — the associated type is what makes that generic.
line_comments: `filter` keeps even numbers, `collect` gathers them into a `Vec<u32>`.
steps.explanation:
`sum`, `filter` and `collect` all work on any iterator because they are written
against the single `Iterator` trait and its associated `Item`. You wrote no trait
code, yet got a sum of `15` and the evens `[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]` — the dividend of
expressing iteration as one trait with an associated type.

steps.title: A Fibonacci iterator
steps.intro:
You implement `Iterator` for real. Build a `Fib` type whose `type Item = u64` and
whose `next` yields the Fibonacci sequence starting at 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, ...
Then `fib_sequence(count)` takes the first `count` values and collects them. The
hidden tests check the vector, but the clean path is a custom iterator plus
`take` and `collect`.

gabarito.justification:
Producing `count = n` values calls `next` `n` times (each O(1)), so time is
**O(n)**, and the collected vector holds `n` numbers, so space is **O(n)**. The
design is the lesson: `type Item = u64` declares what the iterator yields, a
hand-written `next` defines the sequence, and `take`/`collect` — generic over any
`Iterator` — come for free.

units.title: Static vs dynamic dispatch
units.intro:
When code calls a trait method, Rust must decide *which* implementation to run.
With generics and `impl Trait`, it decides at compile time (static dispatch,
monomorphized, inlinable). With `dyn Trait` behind a reference or `Box`, it
decides at run time through a vtable (dynamic dispatch) — slower per call but able
to hold a mix of types in one collection. By the end you sum the areas of a
heterogeneous list of shapes behind `Box<dyn Shape>`.

steps.title: Compile-time or run-time?
steps.intro:
Polymorphism has to resolve to a concrete function somehow. Two strategies trade
off speed against flexibility. Monomorphization bakes a separate copy per type
(fast, bigger binary, one type per call site). Trait objects keep a pointer to a
table of function pointers (one copy, any type at run time, an indirection per
call). Knowing which you are using is the difference between fighting the
compiler and steering it.
steps.body:
## Three ways to pass "something that implements a trait"

**`impl Trait` — static dispatch.** Sugar for a generic; the compiler
monomorphizes and can inline:

```rust
fn announce(x: impl std::fmt::Display) { println!("{x}"); }
fn counter() -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> { (1..=3).map(|n| n * 10) }
```

**`&dyn Trait` / `Box<dyn Trait>` — dynamic dispatch.** A **trait object**: a
pair of pointers (data + vtable). The method called is looked up at run time:

```rust
fn show(item: &dyn std::fmt::Display) { println!("{item}"); }
let shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![/* different types! */];
```

The crucial difference: a `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` can hold `Square`s *and*
`Circle`s together, because each element is just "a pointer to something that is a
`Shape`". A `Vec<T>` where `T: Shape` cannot — a generic resolves to exactly one
concrete type, so every element would have to be the very same shape.

Rule of thumb: reach for static dispatch by default (it is free and inlinable);
reach for `dyn` when you genuinely need a mixed collection or to erase the type.

steps.title: impl Trait in argument position
steps.intro:
`impl Trait` as a parameter type is shorthand for a generic: "accept any type
that implements this". It is static dispatch — the compiler stamps out a copy per
caller type and can inline the call.
steps.prompt:
Write a function taking `impl Display` and call it with two types.

**Why:** `impl Trait` in an argument is a concise generic — static dispatch, no
runtime cost, resolved per call site.
line_comments: `announce` takes `impl Display` — any displayable type (static dispatch).
steps.explanation:
`impl Display` let `announce` accept any displayable type; the compiler produced a
specialised copy for `i32` and another for `&str`. This is static dispatch — each
call resolves at compile time and can be inlined, so it costs nothing extra.

steps.title: impl Trait in return position
steps.intro:
You can also return `impl Trait`: "I return some concrete type that implements
this, but I will not spell out its (often unnameable) name". Iterators built from
closures are the classic case — their real types are impossible to write by hand.
steps.prompt:
Return `impl Iterator<Item = u32>` from a function and loop over it.

**Why:** closure-based iterator types have no writable name; `impl Trait` in the
return lets you hand one back while keeping static dispatch.
line_comments: Returns `impl Iterator<Item = u32>` — some concrete iterator.
A mapped range; its real type is unnameable, so `impl Trait` is ideal.
steps.explanation:
`counter` returned a mapped iterator whose true type is unwriteable, hidden behind
`impl Iterator<Item = u32>`. The loop still used it directly, and dispatch stayed
static — `impl Trait` in return position gives you an opaque-but-concrete type at
zero cost.

steps.title: A heterogeneous Vec of Box<dyn Trait>
steps.intro:
Here is what only dynamic dispatch can do: store different concrete types in one
collection. Each element is a `Box<dyn Shape>` — a pointer to "some `Shape`" — so
a `Square` and a `Circle` live side by side and `area()` is resolved at run time.
steps.prompt:
Build a `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` holding two different types and call a method on
each.

**Why:** a generic `Vec<T>` is one type only. `Box<dyn Shape>` erases the type, so
a single vector can mix implementers — resolved via a vtable at run time.
line_comments: A vector of trait objects — mixed types allowed...
Iterates the trait objects by reference.
`area()` is dispatched at run time via each vtable: prints `4` then `3.14`.
steps.explanation:
The `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` held a `Square` and a `Circle` at once — impossible with
a plain generic, which fixes a single type. Each `s.area()` looked up the right
method at run time through the object's vtable, printing `4` then `3.14`. That is
dynamic dispatch buying you heterogeneity.

steps.title: Dispatch through &dyn Trait
steps.intro:
You do not need a `Box` to get dynamic dispatch — a plain reference `&dyn Trait`
is a trait object too. `show` takes `&dyn Display` and prints whatever it points
at, with the method resolved at run time.
steps.prompt:
Pass values as `&dyn Display` to one function.

**Why:** `&dyn Trait` is the lightest trait object — no allocation, just a
fat pointer — and still dispatches dynamically.
line_comments: `show` takes `&dyn Display` — a borrowed trait object.
Passes a reference to the int as `&dyn Display`; prints `7`.
Passes a reference to the string; prints `seven`.
steps.explanation:
`&dyn Display` turned each borrow into a trait object — a fat pointer carrying the
data and a vtable — and `show` dispatched through it at run time, printing `7` and
`seven`. No `Box`, no allocation: the lightest form of dynamic dispatch.

steps.title: Total area of mixed shapes
steps.intro:
You apply trait objects. Define a `Shape` trait with `area`, implement it for a
`Rect` and a `Circle`, and write `total_area` that sums the areas of a slice of
`Box<dyn Shape>`. The whole point is that the slice may mix rectangles and circles
— dynamic dispatch handles each element's `area` at run time.

gabarito.justification:
`total_area` visits each of the `n` shapes once, summing as it goes, so time is
**O(n)** and extra space is **O(1)**. Each `s.area()` is a dynamic call resolved
through the shape's vtable — which is exactly what lets one slice hold `Rect`s and
`Circle`s together. A generic would have forced a single element type; `Box<dyn
Shape>` erases it.

units.title: Lifetimes: how long a reference is valid
units.intro:
A reference borrows data owned by someone else, and it must never outlive that
data. Lifetimes are the compiler's names for "how long" — usually inferred, but
sometimes you write them (`'a`) to relate the lifetimes of inputs and outputs.
They are purely a compile-time check: no runtime cost, just a guarantee that no
reference ever dangles. By the end you return a borrow of the longest word in a
sentence, with the lifetime tying output to input.

steps.title: Borrows that never dangle
steps.intro:
A dangling pointer — a reference to freed memory — is a classic source of crashes
and exploits in systems languages. Rust abolishes it at compile time with
lifetimes: every reference carries an invisible tag saying how long the data it
points to lives, and the borrow checker refuses any use that could outlast it.
Most of the time this is inferred; naming lifetimes is how you teach the compiler
about relationships it cannot guess.
steps.body:
## `'a`: naming how long a borrow lives

Most references need no annotation — the compiler infers lifetimes (**elision**):

```rust
fn first_line(s: &str) -> &str { s.lines().next().unwrap_or("") }
```

When a function takes several references and returns one, you sometimes must say
how they relate. A named lifetime `'a` does that:

```rust
fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}
```

This reads: "for some lifetime `'a`, both inputs live at least `'a`, and the
result lives no longer than that." The caller cannot keep the result after either
input is gone.

A struct that *holds* a reference must name the lifetime too:

```rust
struct Excerpt<'a> { text: &'a str }
```

Lifetimes are checked entirely at compile time — they vanish from the running
program. They are not about *how long* things live, but about the compiler
proving a reference can never point at data that is already gone.

steps.title: A named lifetime on a function
steps.intro:
When a function returns one of several borrowed inputs, the compiler needs you to
relate their lifetimes. `longest` ties both parameters and the result to one
lifetime `'a`, promising the output lives no longer than the inputs.
steps.prompt:
Write `longest<'a>` returning the longer of two string slices.

**Why:** with two reference inputs and a reference output, elision cannot guess
the relationship — a named `'a` states it.
line_comments: `longest` declares a lifetime `'a`; both inputs and the output share it.
Returns the first borrow when it is at least as long.
steps.explanation:
The annotation `'a` told the compiler that the returned reference lives no longer
than both inputs, so printing `longest(&x, &y)` — `hello` — is provably safe. No
runtime work happened; the lifetime was a compile-time promise that the result
can never dangle.

steps.title: A struct that holds a reference
steps.intro:
If a struct stores a borrow, it must name that borrow's lifetime, so the compiler
can stop the struct from outliving the data. `Excerpt<'a>` keeps a `&'a str`, and
its method returns a slice of the same text.
steps.prompt:
Define a struct holding `&'a str` and give it a method.

**Why:** a struct that borrows must tie its own lifetime to the data it points at,
or it could outlive and dangle.
line_comments: It holds a borrow `&'a str` — valid as long as `'a`.
A method borrowing `self` and returning a slice of the text.
Splits on spaces and takes the first piece (or empty).
steps.explanation:
`Excerpt<'a>` named the lifetime of the string it borrows, so the compiler
guarantees the excerpt can never outlive `novel`. `first_word` returned a slice of
that same text — `Call` — still tied to the original data, never dangling.

steps.title: When lifetimes are inferred
steps.intro:
You usually write no lifetimes at all. For one reference in and one reference out,
the compiler applies elision rules and ties them automatically. `first_line`
returns a borrow of its input without a single `'a` in sight.
steps.prompt:
Write a function that returns a borrow of its one `&str` input — no annotation.

**Why:** with a single reference input, elision infers that the output borrows
from it. Explicit lifetimes would be noise.
line_comments: `first_line` — one reference in, one out; the lifetime is elided (inferred).
Returns the first line, or empty if there is none.
A multi-line string literal (the \\n are newlines).
steps.explanation:
No `'a` appeared, yet the borrow checker still tied the returned slice to the input
`s` through elision, so `first_line(doc)` safely yielded `alpha`. Explicit
lifetimes are only needed when the relationship is ambiguous; here one reference in
and one out made it obvious.

steps.title: Longest word
steps.intro:
You return a borrow safely. Implement `longest_word`, which returns the longest
word of a sentence as a slice *of the input* — no new allocation. The signature
`fn longest_word(sentence: &str) -> &str` relies on lifetime elision to tie the
result to the argument, so the caller can never keep it after the sentence is
gone.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Return the longest word, borrowing from the input:

```rust
pub fn longest_word(sentence: &str) -> &str { ... }
```

Return a slice of `sentence` — the longest whitespace-separated word. For an
empty input, return `""`. If several words tie for longest, return the last of
them (that is what `max_by_key` does).

Examples:

- `longest_word("the quickest brown fox")` → `"quickest"`
- `longest_word("aa bb cc")` → `"cc"` (ties pick the last)
- `longest_word("")` → `""`

**Hint:** `split_whitespace().max_by_key(|w| w.len()).unwrap_or("")`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
One scan over the sentence inspects each word's length, so time is **O(n)** in the
input size; nothing is allocated — the result is a slice *into* the original
string — so extra space is **O(1)**. The elided lifetime ties that returned slice
to `sentence`, which is why the borrow checker proves it can never dangle. `ties
pick the last` because `max_by_key` keeps the later of equal maxima.

units.title: Send, Sync & object safety
units.intro:
The capstone of Rust's type system is fearless concurrency, enforced by two
marker traits. `Send` means a value can be *moved* to another thread; `Sync` means
it can be *shared* (`&T`) across threads. The compiler tracks them automatically
and refuses data races before the program runs. A companion rule — object safety
— decides which traits can become `dyn` trait objects. By the end you sum a vector
in parallel across real OS threads, using only the standard library.

steps.title: Thread safety the compiler checks
steps.intro:
Data races — two threads touching the same memory, one writing, without
synchronisation — are undefined behaviour in most languages and found only by luck
or crashes. Rust promotes thread safety into the type system with two
auto-derived marker traits, so a racy program simply does not compile. Object
safety is a separate but related type-level rule about when a trait can be used
dynamically.
steps.body:
## `Send`, `Sync`, and object safety

Two **marker traits** (no methods — just facts the compiler tracks):

- **`Send`**: the type can be moved to another thread. Almost everything is;
  `Rc<T>` is a notable exception (its counter is not thread-safe).
- **`Sync`**: `&T` can be shared between threads. `T` is `Sync` iff `&T` is
  `Send`.

They are derived automatically, so `thread::spawn` can simply require `Send`:

```rust
let data = vec![1, 2, 3];
let h = std::thread::spawn(move || data.iter().sum::<i32>());
let total = h.join().unwrap();
```

To *share* (not move) data, wrap it in **`Arc<T>`** — an atomically reference-
counted pointer that is `Send + Sync`:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
let shared = Arc::new(vec![10, 20, 30]);
let copy = Arc::clone(&shared); // another thread can read through this
```

**Object safety** decides whether a trait can become `dyn Trait`. A trait is
object-safe when its methods take `self`/`&self`/`&mut self`, are not generic, and
do not return `Self`. `Shape { fn area(&self) -> f64 }` is object-safe — hence the
earlier `Box<dyn Shape>` worked. A trait with a generic method or a `-> Self`
cannot be made into a trait object, because there would be no single vtable to
point at.

steps.title: Move data into a thread (Send)
steps.intro:
Spawning a thread with a `move` closure transfers ownership of the captured data
to the new thread. That transfer is only allowed because the data is `Send`. The
parent waits with `join`, which hands back the thread's result.
steps.prompt:
Move a vector into a spawned thread, compute in it, and join the result.

**Why:** `thread::spawn` requires the closure (and what it captures) to be `Send`.
Moving an owned `Vec` across threads is safe and the compiler verifies it.
line_comments: Owns a vector on this thread.
Spawns a thread; `move` transfers `data` into it (requires `Send`).
Inside the thread: sum the vector.
`join` waits for the thread and unwraps its returned value.
steps.explanation:
The `move` closure carried ownership of `data` into the new thread — legal because
`Vec<i32>` is `Send` — and `join` handed the computed sum, `6`, back to the parent.
The compiler proved there was no shared mutable access, so no data race is
possible.

steps.title: Share data with Arc (Sync)
steps.intro:
To let several threads *read the same* data, wrap it in an `Arc` and clone the
handle for each thread. `Arc<T>` is `Send + Sync`, so sharing is safe; the atomic
counter frees the data when the last handle is gone.
steps.prompt:
Share a vector across three threads with `Arc`, reading one element in each.

**Why:** moving gives one thread ownership; to share read access you need a
thread-safe pointer. `Arc` is exactly that — `Send + Sync`, reference-counted.
line_comments: Wraps the vector in an `Arc` (Send + Sync).
A place to keep the thread handles.
...clone the `Arc` — a cheap new handle to the same data.
Spawn a thread that reads one element and returns it.
...join it and add its returned element.
steps.explanation:
Each thread got its own `Arc` handle to the *same* vector and read one element —
safe because `Arc<Vec<i32>>` is `Send + Sync` and the access was read-only. Summing
the three results gave `60`. `Arc`'s atomic counter dropped the data only after the
last handle was done.

steps.title: Object-safe traits become dyn
steps.intro:
A trait can be used as `dyn Trait` only if it is object-safe: its methods take
`&self` (not generic, not returning `Self`). `Draw` qualifies, so a
`Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>` can hold a mix of shapes and render them through one vtable.
steps.prompt:
Define an object-safe trait and store implementers in a `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>`.

**Why:** object safety is the rule that lets a trait become a trait object. A
simple `&self -> String` method satisfies it.
line_comments: An object-safe method: `&self`, not generic, does not return `Self`.
`render` takes a slice of trait objects (allowed: `Draw` is object-safe).
Maps each to its drawing and joins them with spaces.
A mixed vector of boxed `Draw` objects.
steps.explanation:
Because every `Draw` method takes `&self`, is non-generic and never returns `Self`,
the trait is object-safe — so `Box<dyn Draw>` and `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>` are legal.
`render` dispatched `draw` through each vtable and produced `. --- .`. A trait with
a generic method or a `-> Self` could not be used this way.

steps.title: Parallel sum across threads
steps.intro:
The capstone. Implement `parallel_sum`, which splits a vector into chunks, sums
each chunk on its own OS thread, and combines the partial sums — standard library
only (`std::thread`, `std::sync::Arc`). It must return the same answer as a plain
sequential sum for any number of workers, which is `Send`/`Sync` doing their job:
the data is shared safely and no thread races another.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Sum a vector using several threads:

```rust
pub fn parallel_sum(data: Vec<i64>, workers: usize) -> i64 { ... }
```

Split `data` into roughly equal chunks, sum each chunk on its own thread, and add
the partial sums. The result must equal `data.iter().sum()` for any `workers`.

Rules:

- `workers` of `0` behaves like `1`.
- An empty vector sums to `0`.
- Use only `std::thread` and `std::sync::Arc` — no external crates.

Examples:

- `parallel_sum((1..=100).collect(), 4)` → `5050`
- `parallel_sum(vec![1, 2, 3, 4], 1)` → `10`

**Hint:** wrap the data in an `Arc`, give each thread a start/end range and its own
`Arc::clone`, then sum the values each thread returns from `join`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Every element is added exactly once across all threads, so the total work is
**O(n)**; the `Arc` holds the single shared vector and the handles are `O(workers)`
≤ `O(n)`, so space is **O(n)**. Correctness regardless of `workers` is the lesson:
`Arc<Vec<i64>>` is `Send + Sync`, so each thread safely reads its own disjoint
range, and because no two threads touch the same element there is no data race —
the compiler would reject the code otherwise.

units.title: Threads
units.intro:
A single program can do several things at once by running them on separate
threads of execution. This unit is the start of an advanced concurrency track:
you learn what a thread is, how to start one with `std::thread::spawn`, how to
wait for it with `join`, and how to hand owned data to a thread with `move`.
Everything is standard library, and every result is deterministic.

steps.title: What a thread is
steps.intro:
Until now your programs ran one instruction after another on a single line of
execution. A thread lets a program run more than one such line at the same time.
That power comes with a hazard — shared memory — which the rest of this track
teaches you to tame.
steps.body:
## Threads: doing several things at once

A **thread** is an independent sequence of instructions that the operating system
can run at the same time as other threads. Every program starts with one thread,
the one that runs `main`. You can start more.

Threads of the same program **share the same memory**. That is what makes them
fast to create and able to cooperate — but it is also the source of danger: if two
threads touch the same data at the same time and at least one writes, you have a
**data race**, a bug that is undefined behaviour in most languages.

Rust's job is to make that danger visible at compile time. For now, the mechanics:

```rust
use std::thread;

let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
    // work that runs on a new thread
});
handle.join().unwrap(); // wait for it to finish
```

- **`thread::spawn`** starts a new thread running the given closure and returns a
  **`JoinHandle`**.
- **`join`** blocks the current thread until that thread finishes, and returns
  whatever the closure produced (inside a `Result`, so you `unwrap`).
- A thread outlives the local variables of the function that spawned it, so a
  closure that captures data must usually take ownership with **`move`**. Moving
  owned data into a thread is allowed because the type is `Send`.

Start a thread, give it work, `join` it to collect the answer: that is the whole
shape of the simplest concurrency.

steps.title: Spawn a thread and join it
steps.intro:
The two basic moves: `thread::spawn` starts a thread running a closure, and
`join` waits for it to finish. Without `join`, `main` could end — and tear the
whole program down — before the thread ran.
steps.prompt:
Spawn a thread that prints a line, then wait for it with `join`.

**Why:** a spawned thread runs concurrently with `main`. Joining it guarantees the
thread has finished before the program continues.
line_comments: Spawns a new OS thread running this closure; returns a join handle.
The thread prints its own line.
Closes the closure and the spawn call; the thread is now running.
`join` blocks until the thread finishes; `unwrap` surfaces a panic if any.
Back on the main thread, print that we are done.
steps.explanation:
`spawn` launched the closure on a new thread while `main` kept going; `join` paused
`main` until that thread finished. Because we joined, the program never ended
before the thread's line was printed.

steps.title: Move owned data into a thread
steps.intro:
A thread may run after the spawning function's locals would normally end, so a
closure that uses local data must *own* it. `move` transfers ownership of the
captured values into the thread — allowed because the data is `Send`.
steps.prompt:
Build a `String` on the main thread and `move` it into a spawned thread that uses
it.

**Why:** without `move`, the closure would only borrow `name`, and the borrow could
outlive the owner. `move` gives the thread its own copy of the ownership.
line_comments: Owns a `String` on the main thread.
`move` transfers ownership of `name` into the new thread.
The thread uses the value it now owns.
Closes the closure and spawn call.
Wait for the thread to finish.
steps.explanation:
`move` handed ownership of `name` to the thread, so the closure could safely use it
no matter when the thread actually ran. Moving a `String` across threads is sound
because `String` is `Send`.

steps.title: Two threads, two results, combined
steps.intro:
A thread's closure can *return* a value; `join` hands it back. Spawn two threads
that each compute a partial answer, then join both and combine — a tiny taste of
the parallel-sum pattern.
steps.prompt:
Sum two halves of the work on two separate threads and add the results.

**Why:** each thread owns its own data and returns its own sum; joining both and
adding them gives a result that does not depend on which thread finished first.
line_comments: The first half of the work, owned here.
The second half of the work.
Thread 1 takes `left` (move) and returns its sum.
Thread 2 takes `right` and returns its sum.
Join both threads and add the two partial sums.
steps.explanation:
Each thread owned a disjoint half and returned its partial sum; `join` delivered
both numbers and we added them. The answer, `21`, is the same no matter which
thread finished first — the hallmark of a correct parallel computation.

steps.title: Sum a vector in two threads
steps.intro:
Apply the unit. Implement `sum_in_two_threads`: split the data down the middle,
sum each half on its own thread, and add the two partial sums. The result must
equal a plain sequential sum — threading changes the *how*, never the *what*.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Sum a vector using exactly two threads:

```rust
pub fn sum_in_two_threads(data: Vec<i64>) -> i64 { ... }
```

Split `data` into two halves, sum each half on its own spawned thread, join both,
and return the sum of the partials. The result must equal `data.iter().sum()`.

Rules:

- An empty vector sums to `0`.
- An odd length is fine — the two halves need not be equal.
- Use only `std::thread` — no external crates.

Examples:

- `sum_in_two_threads((1..=100).collect())` → `5050`
- `sum_in_two_threads(vec![1, 2, 3, 4])` → `10`

**Hint:** `Vec::split_off(mid)` gives you the second half as an owned `Vec` and
leaves the first half behind. `move` each half into its own thread.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Every element is summed exactly once across the two threads, so the work is
**O(n)**; the two owned halves together hold `n` elements, so space is **O(n)**.
`split_off` behaves for every length — an empty input leaves both halves empty and
the sum is `0`. Correctness is independent of scheduling because the halves are
disjoint: no element is counted twice and no two threads touch the same memory, so
there is no data race.

units.title: Channels
units.intro:
Sharing memory between threads is dangerous; passing *messages* is safe. A channel
is a one-way pipe: threads send values down it and another thread receives them.
This unit covers `std::sync::mpsc` — create a channel, `send`, `recv`, iterate the
receiver until it closes, and clone the sender for several producers.

steps.title: Communicate by passing messages
steps.intro:
There are two ways for threads to cooperate: share memory and guard it, or send
each other messages and share nothing. Message passing sidesteps a whole class of
bugs, and Rust's standard library gives you a channel to do it.
steps.body:
## Channels: `std::sync::mpsc`

A popular slogan captures the idea: *do not communicate by sharing memory; share
memory by communicating.* A **channel** is a queue with two ends:

```rust
use std::sync::mpsc;

let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
tx.send(42).unwrap();        // producer end
let got = rx.recv().unwrap(); // consumer end, blocks until a value arrives
```

- **`mpsc::channel()`** returns a pair: a **transmitter** `tx` and a **receiver**
  `rx`. The name `mpsc` means *multi-producer, single-consumer*.
- **`tx.send(value)`** pushes a value into the channel. It returns a `Result`
  because sending fails if the receiver is gone.
- **`rx.recv()`** blocks until a value is available and returns it.
- You can loop over the receiver directly — `for value in rx { ... }` — and the
  loop ends automatically when **every** sender has been dropped and the channel
  is empty.
- `tx` is `Clone`: clone it so several producer threads can send into the same
  channel. The receiver only stops iterating once *all* clones are gone.

Because a value is *moved* into the channel on `send` and *moved* out on `recv`,
only one thread ever owns it at a time. There is no shared mutable state, so there
is nothing to race.

steps.title: Send one value, receive it
steps.intro:
The smallest channel program: a thread sends one value, the main thread receives
it. `recv` blocks until the value arrives, so the order is never in doubt.
steps.prompt:
Create a channel, send a value from a spawned thread, and receive it in `main`.

**Why:** `send` moves the value into the channel; `recv` moves it out. Ownership
passes cleanly from one thread to the other — no sharing, no race.
line_comments: Brings the multi-producer, single-consumer channel into scope.
Spawn a thread; `move` gives it the sender `tx`.
The thread sends one value down the channel.
`recv` blocks until a value arrives, then returns it.
steps.explanation:
The value `42` was *moved* into the channel by `send` and *moved* out by `recv`, so
exactly one thread owned it at any moment. `recv` blocked until the value was
there, making the result deterministic.

steps.title: Iterate the receiver until it closes
steps.intro:
A producer can send many values; the consumer loops over the receiver to take them
one by one. The loop ends on its own when the sender is dropped and the channel
drains — no sentinel value needed.
steps.prompt:
Send three numbers from a thread and iterate the receiver to print each.

**Why:** `for value in rx` yields every sent value in order and stops cleanly once
the sender is gone. That is the idiomatic consumer loop.
line_comments: Spawn a producer thread; it owns `tx`.
...one at a time down the channel.
Closes the thread; dropping `tx` will close the channel.
Iterating `rx` yields each value until the channel closes.
steps.explanation:
The producer sent `1, 2, 3` and then ended, which dropped `tx` and closed the
channel; the `for value in rx` loop yielded each value in order and stopped by
itself. No sentinel or counter was needed to know when to stop.

steps.title: Many producers, one consumer
steps.intro:
The `mp` in `mpsc` is multi-producer: clone the sender and each clone can feed the
same channel from its own thread. The receiver keeps going until *every* sender is
dropped, so summing what arrives is deterministic even if the order is not.
steps.prompt:
Clone the sender so two threads each send a value, then sum everything received.

**Why:** cloning `tx` lets several threads produce into one channel. The total of
the received values does not depend on which producer sent first.
line_comments: Clone the sender so a second thread can also send.
Producer 2 owns the clone `tx2` and sends `20`.
A running total on the consumer side.
Iterate until both senders are dropped and the channel closes.
steps.explanation:
Both the original `tx` and its clone `tx2` fed the same channel from different
threads; the receiver only stopped once both were dropped. Summing the arrivals
gave `30` regardless of which producer sent first — order did not affect the total.

steps.title: Producer/consumer sum
steps.intro:
Apply the unit. Implement `sum_via_channel`: a producer thread sends every element
of the vector down a channel, and the consumer sums what it receives. The total
must equal a sequential sum — message passing moves the data safely, one owner at a
time.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Sum a vector by passing its elements through a channel:

```rust
pub fn sum_via_channel(data: Vec<i64>) -> i64 { ... }
```

Spawn a producer thread that sends each element of `data` down an `mpsc` channel.
On the consumer side, receive the values and add them up. The result must equal
`data.iter().sum()`.

Rules:

- An empty vector sums to `0`.
- Use only `std::sync::mpsc` and `std::thread` — no external crates.

Examples:

- `sum_via_channel((1..=100).collect())` → `5050`
- `sum_via_channel(vec![1, 2, 3, 4])` → `10`

**Hint:** move `data` into the producer thread and `send` each element. On the main
thread, sum the receiver with `rx.iter().sum()` — the iterator ends when the
producer drops its sender.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Each element is sent once and received once, so the work is **O(n)**; the channel
buffers values in flight, bounded by `n`, so space is **O(n)**. The result is
deterministic because a channel moves one value at a time — there is no shared
mutable state to race — and `rx.iter()` ends exactly when the producer drops `tx`,
so every element is accounted for, including zero elements for an empty input.

units.title: Shared state
units.intro:
Sometimes threads really must share one piece of mutable state. The safe tool is
`Arc<Mutex<T>>`: an `Arc` shares ownership across threads and a `Mutex` guarantees
only one thread touches the value at a time. This unit builds a counter incremented
by many threads and a vector filled in parallel — always with a correct total.

steps.title: One value, many threads, no races
steps.intro:
When several threads must read and write the *same* value, you need two things at
once: shared ownership so every thread may hold the value, and mutual exclusion so
only one writes at a time. `Arc` and `Mutex` provide exactly those two guarantees.
steps.body:
## `Arc<Mutex<T>>`: shared, synchronised state

Two separate problems, two tools, combined:

- **`Arc<T>`** — *atomically reference-counted* — lets many threads **share
  ownership** of one value. Clone it (cheaply) and each thread holds a handle; the
  value is freed when the last handle is dropped. `Arc` alone only grants shared
  *read* access.
- **`Mutex<T>`** — *mutual exclusion* — guards a value so only one thread can
  access it at a time. Calling **`lock()`** blocks until the lock is free and
  returns a **guard**; while you hold the guard you have exclusive access, and the
  lock releases automatically when the guard is dropped.

Put them together — `Arc<Mutex<T>>` — to share one mutable value safely:

```rust
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};

let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));
let c = Arc::clone(&counter);        // a handle for another thread
let mut n = c.lock().unwrap();       // exclusive access
*n += 1;                             // safe mutation
```

- `lock()` returns a `Result` (it fails only if another thread panicked while
  holding the lock), so you `unwrap`.
- Keep the critical section — the time you hold the guard — as short as possible;
  the lock serialises threads, so long holds throw away parallelism.

With the mutex in place, the final count is exact no matter how the threads
interleave: every increment happens under the lock, so none is ever lost.

steps.title: Lock a Mutex to change a value
steps.intro:
Before adding threads, see the `Mutex` alone: `lock()` hands you a guard with
exclusive access, and dropping the guard releases the lock. An inner scope makes
the release point obvious.
steps.prompt:
Guard an integer with a `Mutex`, increment it under the lock, then read it back.

**Why:** `lock()` returns a guard that gives exclusive access; the lock is held
only while the guard lives. Scoping the guard controls exactly when it releases.
line_comments: A `Mutex` guarding an integer, starting at 0.
Open an inner scope so the lock releases at its end.
`lock` returns a guard giving exclusive access to the value.
Change the value through the guard.
Leaving the scope drops the guard and unlocks the mutex.
Lock again to read, and print `1`.
steps.explanation:
`lock()` gave exclusive access through a guard; mutating `*guard` changed the
protected value, and leaving the inner scope released the lock so the final `lock`
could read it. Holding the guard for the shortest span keeps other threads waiting
as little as possible.

steps.title: A counter shared by many threads
steps.intro:
Now the real thing: wrap the counter in `Arc<Mutex<i32>>`, clone a handle for each
thread, and have every thread lock and increment. The mutex serialises the writes,
so no increment is lost and the final total is exact.
steps.prompt:
Share a counter across four threads with `Arc<Mutex<_>>`; each thread adds one.

**Why:** `Arc` lets every thread own a handle to the same counter; the `Mutex`
ensures their increments never collide. The result is deterministic: exactly four.
line_comments: `Arc` shares the `Mutex` across threads; the `Mutex` guards the count.
Each worker gets its own `Arc` handle to the same mutex.
Spawn a thread capturing that handle...
The lock releases here; store the handle.
Lock once more to read and print `4`.
steps.explanation:
Four threads each locked the shared mutex and added one; because the lock
serialised them, not a single increment was lost and the total was exactly `4`.
Without the mutex the compiler would have rejected the shared mutable access.

steps.title: Fill a shared vector in parallel
steps.intro:
A mutex can guard any type, not just a number. Here threads push into a shared
`Vec`. The order they push is unpredictable, so we sort the result to get a stable,
deterministic output.
steps.prompt:
Have three threads push their index into a shared vector, then sort and print it.

**Why:** the mutex makes concurrent `push` calls safe; sorting afterwards removes
the only non-determinism — the arrival order — leaving a stable result.
line_comments: A shared, mutex-guarded vector, shared via `Arc`.
...clone the `Arc` handle to the shared vector.
...locks the vector and pushes its index.
Copy the shared vector out under the lock.
Sort so the output is deterministic regardless of thread order.
steps.explanation:
Each thread locked the vector to push its index safely; because threads can finish
in any order, we sorted the copy before printing. The result `[0, 1, 2]` is stable
across runs even though the push order is not.

steps.title: Parallel counter
steps.intro:
Apply the unit. Implement `parallel_counter(n_threads, per_thread)`: start
`n_threads` threads that each add `1` to a shared counter `per_thread` times, then
return the final total. With `Arc<Mutex<_>>` guarding the count, the answer is
always exactly `n_threads * per_thread`.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Count in parallel with a shared, locked counter:

```rust
pub fn parallel_counter(n_threads: usize, per_thread: usize) -> i64 { ... }
```

Create a counter shared by `n_threads` threads. Each thread increments it
`per_thread` times. After all threads finish, return the counter's value. It must
equal `n_threads * per_thread`.

Rules:

- `n_threads` or `per_thread` of `0` yields a total of `0`.
- Use only `std::sync::{Arc, Mutex}` and `std::thread` — no external crates.

Examples:

- `parallel_counter(4, 1000)` → `4000`
- `parallel_counter(3, 7)` → `21`

**Hint:** wrap the count in `Arc::new(Mutex::new(0i64))`, give each thread an
`Arc::clone`, and inside each thread loop `per_thread` times, locking and adding
one. Join every thread before reading the total.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
There are exactly `n_threads * per_thread` increments, each done once under the
lock, so the work is **O(n_threads * per_thread)**; the only extra storage is one
join handle per thread, so space is **O(n_threads)**. Correctness is independent of
scheduling: every increment happens inside the mutex's critical section, so no two
overlap and none is lost — the total is always the product, including `0` when
either factor is `0`.

units.title: Parallelism
units.intro:
The payoff of the whole track: split a large job across threads, let them work on
disjoint pieces, and combine the pieces into one answer. This unit uses
`thread::scope` to borrow local data without `Arc`, divides a vector into chunks,
and finishes by counting primes in parallel — always with a deterministic result.

steps.title: Divide the work, combine the answers
steps.intro:
Concurrency is about *dealing with* many things at once; parallelism is about
*doing* many things at once to go faster. The recipe is always the same: split the
input into independent parts, process the parts on different threads, and reduce
their results into one.
steps.body:
## Data parallelism: split, compute, combine

To make a big computation faster with threads, give each thread a **disjoint**
slice of the data. Because the slices do not overlap, the threads never touch the
same memory — no locks, no races — and the partial results combine into the whole:

1. **Split** the data into `k` roughly equal chunks.
2. **Compute** a partial result for each chunk on its own thread.
3. **Combine** (reduce) the partials into the final answer.

Because a thread must not outlive the data it borrows, sharing owned data usually
needs `Arc`. But the standard library offers a lighter tool for the common case
where the data outlives the threads: **`thread::scope`**.

```rust
use std::thread;

let data = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
let total: i32 = thread::scope(|s| {
    let h = s.spawn(|| data.iter().sum::<i32>());
    h.join().unwrap()
});
```

- Inside `thread::scope`, scoped threads created with **`s.spawn`** may **borrow**
  local variables directly — no `move`, no `Arc` — because the scope guarantees
  every scoped thread finishes before `scope` returns.
- Gathering the partials in a fixed order (for example, by chunk index) makes the
  combined result **deterministic**: the final answer never depends on which thread
  happened to finish first.

Split into disjoint chunks, compute in parallel, reduce in order: that is the
engine of data parallelism.

steps.title: Borrow local data with thread::scope
steps.intro:
`thread::scope` lets a scoped thread borrow a local value directly, because the
scope guarantees the thread finishes before the borrowed data can go away. No
`move`, no `Arc` — just a borrow.
steps.prompt:
Sum a local vector inside a scoped thread and read the result out.

**Why:** scoped threads may borrow the surrounding function's locals, because
`thread::scope` joins them before returning. It is the lightest way to fan out over
borrowed data.
line_comments: Some data owned on the main thread.
`thread::scope` lets scoped threads borrow local data safely.
A scoped thread borrows `data` (no `move`, no `Arc`) and sums it.
Join it and store the result.
The scope ends; all scoped threads are guaranteed finished here.
steps.explanation:
The scoped thread borrowed `data` directly — allowed because `thread::scope`
guarantees it finishes before the scope returns, so the borrow can never dangle.
That removed the need for `move` or `Arc` entirely.

steps.title: Split into chunks and reduce in order
steps.intro:
The core data-parallel pattern: cut the data into disjoint chunks, sum each on its
own scoped thread, then gather the partials by index. Gathering in index order is
what makes the final sum deterministic.
steps.prompt:
Divide ten numbers into two chunks, sum each on a thread, and reduce the partials.

**Why:** disjoint chunks mean no shared memory and no races; collecting the
partials by index gives the same total every run, independent of thread timing.
line_comments: Ten numbers to add in parallel.
Each worker handles an equal chunk of the data.
A slot per worker for its partial sum.
Open a scope so threads may borrow `data`.
...take a disjoint slice of the data (no overlap, so no races).
Spawn a scoped thread that sums its slice; `move` captures the slice reference.
...storing each partial in its slot (deterministic order).
The scope ends; all workers have finished.
Reduce the partials into the final total.

steps.title: Count matches in parallel
steps.intro:
Parallelism is not only for sums: any per-element test that is combined by addition
works. Here two threads count the even numbers in two halves, and the counts add up
to the whole — a direct rehearsal for the prime-counting challenge.
steps.prompt:
Count the even numbers in `1..=100` using two threads over two halves.

**Why:** counting matches is an associative reduction, so splitting the range and
adding the per-half counts gives the same answer as scanning it all at once.
line_comments: A helper: is this number even?
True when the remainder on division by two is zero.
Open a scope and capture its two results.
Thread 1 counts evens in the left half.
Thread 2 counts evens in the right half.
The scope block yields the pair of partial counts.
The scope ends; both threads have finished.
Prints the total count of evens: `50`.
steps.explanation:
Each thread counted evens in its own half, and the two counts added to `50` — the
same as counting the whole range. Because counting is an associative reduction,
splitting the work left the answer unchanged.

steps.title: Count primes in parallel
steps.intro:
The capstone of the concurrency track. Implement `count_primes_parallel(upto,
workers)`: count the prime numbers in `2..=upto` by splitting the range across
`workers` threads and summing the per-chunk counts. The answer must match a
sequential count exactly — parallelism must change only the speed, never the result.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Count primes using several threads:

```rust
pub fn count_primes_parallel(upto: u64, workers: usize) -> usize { ... }
```

Count how many primes are in `2..=upto`. Split the candidates across `workers`
threads, count the primes in each chunk, and sum the counts. The result must equal
a single-threaded count.

Rules:

- `upto < 2` yields `0`.
- `workers` of `0` behaves like `1`.
- Use only `std::thread` (and `std::sync::Arc` if you like) — no external crates.

Examples:

- `count_primes_parallel(10, 4)` → `4` (2, 3, 5, 7)
- `count_primes_parallel(100, 7)` → `25`

**Hint:** build the candidates `2..=upto`, split them into chunks, and give each
thread a chunk to count with a simple `is_prime` test. Sum what the threads return.
A trial-division `is_prime` (test divisors up to `sqrt(n)`) is plenty.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Each of the `n = upto - 1` candidates is tested once with trial division up to its
square root, so the work is **O(n * sqrt(n))**; the shared `Arc<Vec<u64>>` holds the
`n` candidates, so space is **O(n)**. The count is deterministic because the chunks
are disjoint — every candidate is tested exactly once, on exactly one thread — so no
primality test is duplicated or lost, and summing the per-chunk counts yields the
same total as a single-threaded scan, for any number of workers.

units.title: Stacks and Queues
units.intro:
Two of the most useful containers in programming are built straight from the
standard library. A **stack** is last-in, first-out: `Vec` already is one — `push`
puts an item on top, `pop` takes the top back off. A **queue** is first-in,
first-out: `VecDeque` adds at the back with `push_back` and removes from the front
with `pop_front`. This unit uses both, then checks balanced brackets with a stack.

steps.title: Last in first out, first in first out
steps.intro:
A stack and a queue differ only in *which end* you take from. Pick the stack when
you want to undo the most recent thing first; pick the queue when you want to serve
things in arrival order.
steps.body:
## `Vec` is a stack

A `Vec` grows and shrinks at its end, which is exactly a **stack** — last in, first
out (LIFO). `push` adds to the top; `pop` removes the top and returns it as an
`Option` (`None` when empty):

```rust
let mut stack = Vec::new();
stack.push(1);
stack.push(2);
assert_eq!(stack.pop(), Some(2)); // the last pushed comes off first
```

## `VecDeque` is a queue

A **queue** serves in arrival order — first in, first out (FIFO). `VecDeque` is a
double-ended queue that can push and pop at *both* ends cheaply. Use `push_back` to
enqueue and `pop_front` to dequeue:

```rust
use std::collections::VecDeque;

let mut queue = VecDeque::new();
queue.push_back("a");
queue.push_back("b");
assert_eq!(queue.pop_front(), Some("a")); // the first enqueued leaves first
```

- Both `pop` and `pop_front` return `Option`, so an empty container yields `None`
  instead of panicking — handle that case with `while let Some(x) = ...` or a match.
- A stack reverses order (the last in leaves first); a queue preserves it.

Reach for a stack to process *most recent first* (undo, bracket matching,
depth-first search) and a queue for *fair, in-order* processing (task lists,
breadth-first search).

steps.title: Use a Vec as a stack
steps.intro:
A `Vec` is already a stack: `push` adds to the top and `pop` removes the top,
returning it as an `Option`. Three pushes then one pop shows the last-in,
first-out order directly.
steps.prompt:
Push three numbers onto a `Vec`, pop one, and print the popped value and the rest.

**Why:** `push`/`pop` operate at the end of the `Vec`, which is the defining
behaviour of a stack — the most recently added item is the first one back out.
line_comments: An empty `Vec` — we will use it as a stack.
`pop` removes and returns the top element as an `Option`.
steps.explanation:
`pop` returned `Some(3)` — the value pushed most recently — and left `[1, 2]`
behind. That last-in, first-out behaviour is what makes a `Vec` a ready-made stack.

steps.title: Use a VecDeque as a queue
steps.intro:
`VecDeque` is a double-ended queue. Enqueue at the back with `push_back` and
dequeue from the front with `pop_front`, and items leave in the same order they
arrived — first in, first out.
steps.prompt:
Enqueue three strings with `push_back`, dequeue one with `pop_front`, and print both.

**Why:** a queue serves in arrival order; taking from the front while adding at the
back preserves that order, unlike a stack which reverses it.
line_comments: `pop_front` dequeues from the front as an `Option`.
steps.explanation:
`pop_front` returned `Some("a")` — the item enqueued first — leaving `b` and `c` in
order. A queue preserves arrival order, which is exactly what `push_back` paired
with `pop_front` gives you.

steps.title: Drain a stack to reverse
steps.intro:
Popping a stack until it is empty visits the items in reverse order. A
`while let Some(x) = stack.pop()` loop is the idiomatic way to drain it, because
`pop` yields `None` exactly when the stack runs out.
steps.prompt:
Pop a four-element stack until empty, collecting into a new vector.

**Why:** each `pop` takes the current top, so draining a stack naturally reverses
it — the first item out is the one that was on top (pushed last).
line_comments: `while let` keeps popping until the stack is empty.
steps.explanation:
The loop ran until `pop` returned `None`, pulling `4, 3, 2, 1` off the top in turn.
Draining a stack is a tidy way to reverse a sequence without any index arithmetic.

steps.title: Balanced brackets
steps.intro:
The classic use of a stack. Implement `balanced_parens(s)`: return `true` when every
opening bracket `(`, `[`, `{` has a matching closing bracket of the same kind, in the
right nesting order. A stack remembers what is still open — push on an opener, and on
a closer check that the top is its match.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Check that brackets are balanced using a stack:

```rust
pub fn balanced_parens(s: &str) -> bool { ... }
```

Return `true` when the brackets `()`, `[]`, `{}` in `s` are balanced and correctly
nested; `false` otherwise. Any other character is ignored.

Rules:

- An empty string is balanced (`true`).
- Push each opener onto a stack; on each closer, pop and check it matches.
- A closer with an empty stack, or a mismatched top, means `false`.
- Left-over openers at the end (non-empty stack) mean `false`.

Examples:

- `balanced_parens("([{}])")` → `true`
- `balanced_parens("([)]")` → `false` (wrong nesting)
- `balanced_parens("(((")` → `false` (never closed)

**Hint:** iterate `s.chars()`. On `(`, `[`, `{` push the character. On `)`, `]`, `}`
pop and compare with the expected opener; return `false` on any mismatch or empty
pop. At the end the string is balanced exactly when the stack is empty.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Each character is examined once and triggers at most one `push` or `pop`, so the time
is **O(n)** in the length of `s`. The stack holds at most one entry per unmatched
opener, so worst-case space is **O(n)** (a string of all openers). Correctness follows
from the invariant that the stack always holds exactly the still-open brackets in
nesting order: a closer must match the top, and a fully balanced string ends with an
empty stack.

units.title: Linked Lists
units.intro:
A linked list is the first data structure you build from pointers rather than a
contiguous block. In Rust the shape is `Option<Box<Node>>`: each node owns the next
through a `Box`, and `None` marks the end. This unit builds a singly linked list —
push to the front, pop from the front, measure its length — then reverses a sequence
by pushing every item to the front.

steps.title: Nodes that own the next node
steps.intro:
A linked list stores each value in its own node, and each node *owns* the rest of
the list. Because ownership must have a known size, the link goes through a `Box` —
a pointer to heap data — and ends with `None`.
steps.body:
## The shape: `Option<Box<Node>>`

A node holds a value and a link to the next node. The link is
`Option<Box<Node>>`: `Some(box)` points at another node, `None` ends the list. The
`Box` is essential — without it the type would contain itself and have infinite
size:

```rust
struct Node {
    val: i32,
    next: Option<Box<Node>>,
}
```

## Push to the front

The cheapest insertion is at the head: make a new node whose `next` is the old
head, then make it the new head. `Option::take` swaps the old head out (leaving
`None` in its place) so it can be moved into the new node:

```rust
let mut head: Option<Box<Node>> = None;
head = Some(Box::new(Node { val: 1, next: head.take() }));
head = Some(Box::new(Node { val: 2, next: head.take() })); // 2 -> 1 -> end
```

- `Box<Node>` owns one node on the heap; dropping the head drops the whole chain.
- `head.take()` is the idiom for moving an owned value *out* of an `Option` while
  leaving it valid (`None`) — exactly what you need when re-linking.
- To walk the list, follow `&node.next` with a `while let Some(node) = cur` loop.

Push-front then walk is the backbone of every operation in this unit — including
reversing a sequence, which push-front does almost for free.

steps.title: Build a list by pushing to the front
steps.intro:
Pushing each value to the front links it ahead of the previous head. `head.take()`
moves the old head out of the `Option` (leaving `None`) so it can become the new
node's `next`. Walking the result shows the order reversed.
steps.prompt:
Push `1, 2, 3` to the front of a list, then walk it collecting the values.

**Why:** `Option::take` lets you move the owned head out while leaving the `Option`
valid, which is exactly what re-linking the head needs; push-front reverses order.
line_comments: A list node: a value plus an optional boxed next node.
`Option<Box<Node>>` — `Some` for a next node, `None` for the end.
...push it to the front: the old head becomes the new node's `next`.
Collect the values into a vector.
Start a walking reference at the head.
`while let` follows the chain while a node is present.
Prints `[3, 2, 1]` — push-front reverses the input order.
steps.explanation:
Each value was linked ahead of the previous head, so walking from the head produced
`[3, 2, 1]` — the reverse of the input. That is the whole idea behind the reversal
challenge: push every item to the front.

steps.title: Measure a list's length
steps.intro:
Length is a walk: start a reference at the head and follow `next` links, counting
one per node, until you reach `None`. Reassigning the walking reference to
`&node.next` is how you move along the chain without taking ownership.
steps.prompt:
Write `len` that counts the nodes in a borrowed list, and call it on a two-node list.

**Why:** walking by shared reference (`&Option<Box<Node>>`) visits every node without
moving or mutating the list, so the list is still usable afterwards.
line_comments: The link to the rest of the list, or `None`.
`len` walks the chain from a borrowed head.
`while let` continues while there is a node.
Move the reference to the next link.
The tail node, ending the list.
The head owns the two-node list.
Prints `2` — the list has two nodes.
steps.explanation:
`len` followed the `next` links from the head, counting two nodes before reaching
`None`. Because it borrowed the list (`&`), the list was untouched and still usable
after the call.

steps.title: Pop the front node
steps.intro:
Popping the front means taking the head out, reading its value, and promoting its
`next` to be the new head. `head.take()` removes the head (leaving `None`), and the
node it hands back owns the rest of the list through its `next` field.
steps.prompt:
Pop the front of a two-node list, printing the popped value and the new front.

**Why:** `take` moves the head node out so you own it; its `next` field *is* the
remainder of the list, so assigning it back to `head` drops exactly one node.
line_comments: The link to the next node, or `None`.
The head node holding `10`, linked to `a`.
Where the popped value will go.
`take` removes the head node, leaving `head` as `None`.
Reattach the rest of the list as the new head.
Prints `Some(10) Some(20)` — popped value, then the new front.
steps.explanation:
`take` handed back the head node holding `10`; its `next` field — the rest of the
list — became the new head, so the front is now `20`. Popping the front is just
owning the head and promoting its `next`.

steps.title: Reverse with a linked list
steps.intro:
