Put push-front to work. Implement `reverse_list(items)`: build a singly linked list
by pushing each item to the front, then walk the list collecting the values into a
`Vec`. Because every push puts the item ahead of the rest, the collected order is the
reverse of the input — a linked list reverses a sequence for free.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Reverse a sequence using a linked list:

```rust
pub fn reverse_list(items: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<i32> { ... }
```

Build a singly linked list of `Option<Box<Node>>` by pushing each element of `items`
to the **front**, then walk the list from the head and collect the values into a
`Vec`. The result is `items` reversed.

Rules:

- An empty input yields an empty `Vec`.
- Use your own `Node` type with an `Option<Box<Node>>` link — no `.rev()` shortcut.
- Push-front: the new node's `next` is the old head.

Examples:

- `reverse_list(vec![1, 2, 3, 4])` → `vec![4, 3, 2, 1]`
- `reverse_list(vec![7])` → `vec![7]`

**Hint:** start with `head = None`. For each `x`, set
`head = Some(Box::new(Node { val: x, next: head.take() }))`. Then walk with
`while let Some(node) = cur { out.push(node.val); cur = node.next; }`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Building the list does one `push_front` per item (constant work each), and walking it
visits each node once, so the total time is **O(n)**. The list owns one heap node per
element plus the output vector, giving **O(n)** space. Each push links the new value
ahead of the previous head, so the head-to-tail order is the reverse of the insertion
order — walking from the head collects the input reversed.

units.title: Maps and Sets
units.intro:
Hashing gives you two indispensable tools in near-constant time. A `HashMap<K, V>`
associates keys with values — perfect for counting how often each thing appears. A
`HashSet<T>` stores only keys — perfect for dedup and fast membership tests. This
unit counts frequencies, de-duplicates, tests membership, and finishes with two-sum
using a map to find a pair in a single pass.

steps.title: Key to value, and keys alone
steps.intro:
A map remembers a value for each key; a set remembers only that a key is present.
Both answer *"have I seen this?"* in roughly constant time, which turns many
quadratic scans into single passes.
steps.body:
## `HashMap`: count with the entry API

A `HashMap<K, V>` looks up, inserts, and updates by key in average O(1). The
`entry` API is the clean way to update-or-insert: `entry(k).or_insert(0)` hands you
a mutable reference to the value for `k`, creating it with a default first if
needed:

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

let mut counts: HashMap<&str, i32> = HashMap::new();
for w in ["a", "b", "a"] {
    *counts.entry(w).or_insert(0) += 1; // count occurrences
}
assert_eq!(counts["a"], 2);
```

## `HashSet`: membership and dedup

A `HashSet<T>` is a map with no values — it stores unique keys. `insert` returns
`false` if the item was already present, and `contains` tests membership in O(1).
Collecting an iterator into a `HashSet` drops duplicates:

```rust
use std::collections::HashSet;

let set: HashSet<i32> = [3, 1, 2, 3].iter().copied().collect();
assert_eq!(set.len(), 3); // the duplicate 3 is gone
```

- Iteration order of a `HashMap`/`HashSet` is **unspecified** — never print one
  directly if you need stable output. Collect into a `Vec` and `sort` first.
- A hash map lets you trade memory for speed: remember what you have seen so you
  never have to rescan for it.

Counting, de-duplicating, and *"have I seen the complement?"* lookups are the three
patterns that carry this unit into the two-sum challenge.

steps.title: Count frequencies with a HashMap
steps.intro:
The `entry` API counts in one line: `entry(w).or_insert(0)` gives a mutable slot
(created at `0` the first time), and `+= 1` bumps it. Because map order is
unspecified, collect into a `Vec` and `sort` before printing.
line_comments: A map from word to its running count.
Collect the pairs into a vector so we can order them.
Sort for deterministic output (map order is unspecified).
steps.explanation:
The `entry` API counted each word in a single pass, and sorting the pairs made the
output stable: `[("a", 3), ("b", 2), ("c", 1)]`. Never print a map directly — its
iteration order is deliberately randomised.

steps.title: De-duplicate with a HashSet
steps.intro:
Collecting into a `HashSet` keeps one copy of each value and discards the rest.
Since set order is unspecified, move the uniques into a `Vec` and `sort` for a
stable result.
steps.prompt:
Collect numbers with duplicates into a `HashSet`, then print the sorted unique values.

**Why:** a set stores each key once, so `collect` into a `HashSet` is the shortest
way to dedup; sorting afterwards restores a predictable order for output.
line_comments: Collecting into a `HashSet` drops duplicates automatically.
Move the unique values into a vector.
Sort for deterministic output (set order is unspecified).
steps.explanation:
Collecting into the set left one of each value; sorting the result gave
`[1, 2, 3, 4]`. A `HashSet` is the quickest route to unique elements when you do not
need to preserve the original order.

steps.title: Test membership with contains
steps.intro:
`HashSet::contains` answers membership in average O(1). Building a set from one group
and testing another against it beats a nested loop, which would be O(n*m).
steps.prompt:
Build a set from one group of numbers and count how many of a second group are in it.

**Why:** a set membership test is near-constant time, so checking each element of the
second group against the set is linear overall — not quadratic.
line_comments: Build a set from the first group of numbers.
A second group to test against the set.
`contains` is O(1) membership; count how many of `b` are in `a`.
steps.explanation:
Each element of `b` was tested against the set in constant time, so the whole count
was linear and gave `2`. Pre-loading one side into a `HashSet` turns a quadratic
cross-check into a single pass.

steps.title: Two-sum with a HashMap
steps.intro:
The interview classic, solved in one pass. Implement `two_sum(nums, target)`: find
two *distinct* indices whose values add up to `target`. As you scan, a `HashMap`
remembers each value you have already seen and where; for the current value you look
up its complement (`target - n`) — if it is in the map, you have your pair.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Find a pair of indices that sum to the target:

```rust
pub fn two_sum(nums: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<(usize, usize)> { ... }
```

Return `Some((i, j))` with `i < j` and `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`, or `None` if no
such pair exists. Return the first such pair found while scanning left to right, with
the smaller index first.

Rules:

- Each index may be used once; the two indices must differ.
- Do it in a single pass with a `HashMap` from value to index — not a nested loop.
- An empty or single-element slice yields `None`.

Examples:

- `two_sum(&[2, 7, 11, 15], 9)` → `Some((0, 1))`
- `two_sum(&[3, 2, 4], 6)` → `Some((1, 2))`
- `two_sum(&[1, 2, 3], 100)` → `None`

**Hint:** keep a `HashMap<i32, usize>` of values you have seen. For each `(i, n)`,
compute `need = target - n`; if `need` is in the map at index `j`, return
`Some((j, i))`. Otherwise record `n -> i` (only if absent) and continue.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The slice is scanned once, and each step does an average O(1) map lookup and insert,
so the total time is **O(n)**. The map stores at most one entry per element, giving
**O(n)** space. For the current index `i`, the complement `target - nums[i]` is looked
up among the earlier values; if present at index `j`, then `j < i`, so `(j, i)` is
returned smaller-index-first and is the first such pair in scan order.

units.title: Binary Search Trees
units.intro:
A binary search tree keeps values ordered by *where* they sit: everything smaller
than a node goes left, everything larger goes right. That invariant makes `insert`
and `contains` follow a single path down the tree, and an in-order traversal reads
the values back in sorted order. This unit builds a BST of `i32` with
`Option<Box<Node>>`, then returns a sorted, de-duplicated sequence from raw inserts.

steps.title: Smaller left, larger right
steps.intro:
The binary-search-tree invariant is one rule applied at every node: left subtree
holds smaller values, right subtree holds larger ones. Keep that rule and search,
insertion, and sorted output all fall out naturally.

steps.title: Insert into a binary search tree
steps.prompt:
Insert `5, 3, 8` into an empty tree and print the root with its two children.

**Why:** comparing at each node and stepping one way keeps every value on the correct
side, so the first value inserted becomes the root and the rest hang beneath it.
line_comments: A binary-search-tree node with left and right children.
`insert` places `v` in the subtree rooted at `root`.
Empty slot: plant a new leaf node here.
Smaller than this node: recurse into the left child.
Greater than this node: recurse into the right child.
Equal: already present, so do nothing (duplicates ignored).
Unwrap the root (the first value inserted).
Prints `5 3 8` — root, left child, right child.
steps.explanation:
`5` became the root; `3` went left because it is smaller and `8` went right because
it is larger, printing `5 3 8`. Each insert followed one comparison per level to
reach its empty slot.

steps.title: In-order traversal reads sorted
steps.intro:
An in-order walk visits left subtree, node, then right subtree. Because the BST
invariant puts smaller values left and larger values right, this emits the values in
ascending order — no sorting step required.
steps.prompt:
Walk a small tree (root `5`, children `3` and `8`) in order and collect the values.

**Why:** visiting left-node-right at every node interleaves the subtrees so that each
value is emitted only after everything smaller than it — i.e. in sorted order.
line_comments: A binary-search-tree node with two child links.
`walk` does an in-order traversal, appending values to `out`.
If there is a node here...
...visit the entire left subtree first (smaller values).
Then visit the right subtree (larger values).
`leaf` builds a childless node wrapped in `Some`.
Prints `[3, 5, 8]` — in-order visits a BST in sorted order.
steps.explanation:
Visiting left, then node, then right produced `[3, 5, 8]` — ascending — straight from
the tree's shape. The BST invariant is what makes in-order traversal a sort.

steps.title: Search a binary search tree
steps.intro:
`contains` mirrors `insert`: compare at each node and step one way. Equal means
found; smaller means go left; larger means go right; falling off the tree (`None`)
means absent. Only one path is ever examined.
steps.prompt:
Search a small tree for a value that is present and one that is not, printing both.

**Why:** because smaller values are always left and larger always right, a search can
discard half the remaining tree at every step — it never needs to look at both sides.
line_comments: Ran off the tree: not found.
Target is smaller: search the left subtree only.
Otherwise it is larger: search the right subtree.
Prints `true false` — `8` is present, `4` is not.
steps.explanation:
Searching for `8` stepped right to a match; searching for `4` stepped left and ran off
the tree, giving `true false`. Each search followed a single root-to-leaf path.

steps.title: Sort by building a BST
steps.intro:
Bring insert and in-order traversal together. Implement
`sorted_from_inserts(items)`: insert every element into a binary search tree, then
return its in-order traversal. The invariant does the sorting, and the equal-value
case being ignored means duplicates drop out — so the result is the input's values,
sorted and unique.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Produce a sorted, de-duplicated sequence via a BST:

```rust
pub fn sorted_from_inserts(items: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<i32> { ... }
```

Insert each element of `items` into a binary search tree (smaller left, larger
right, equal ignored), then return the in-order traversal as a `Vec<i32>`.

Rules:

- The output is ascending and contains no duplicates.
- Empty input yields an empty `Vec`.
- Build a real BST with `Option<Box<Node>>` — do not call `sort`/`dedup`.

Examples:

- `sorted_from_inserts(vec![5, 3, 8, 1, 4])` → `vec![1, 3, 4, 5, 8]`
- `sorted_from_inserts(vec![2, 2, 1, 3, 3])` → `vec![1, 2, 3]`

**Hint:** reuse the `insert` (smaller left, larger right, equal does nothing) and the
in-order `walk` (left, node, right) from the drills. Insert all items, then walk the
root into an output `Vec`.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.time: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst
gabarito.justification:
Each insert costs O(height): about **O(log n)** on a balanced tree but **O(n)** on
already-sorted input, so the build is **O(n log n)** average and **O(n^2)** worst case;
the in-order walk is **O(n)**. The tree holds at most one node per distinct value, so
space is **O(n)**. The BST invariant (smaller left, larger right) makes the in-order
traversal ascending, and the equal case doing nothing drops duplicates, so the output
is sorted and unique.

units.title: Sorting and Searching
units.intro:
Two algorithms are worth implementing by hand at least once. **Merge sort** divides
a vector in half, sorts each half, and merges the two sorted halves in linear time —
O(n log n), and stable. **Binary search** halves its search window each step to find
a value in a sorted slice in O(log n). This unit builds the merge and the search
piece by piece, then assembles a full merge sort.

steps.title: Divide, merge, and halve
steps.intro:
Merge sort and binary search are both *divide and conquer*: split the problem in
half and recombine (or discard) half the work each step. That halving is where the
logarithm in their running time comes from.

steps.title: Merge two sorted slices
steps.intro:
Merging is the heart of merge sort. Two cursors walk the inputs; at each step the
smaller front is taken, and `<=` (favour the left on ties) keeps equal elements in
their original order — a stable merge. Leftovers are appended at the end.
steps.prompt:
Merge `[1, 3, 5]` and `[2, 4, 6]` into one sorted vector.

**Why:** because both inputs are already sorted, comparing only their fronts is
enough to emit the next-smallest value, so the whole merge is linear in the total length.
line_comments: `merge` combines two already-sorted slices into one sorted vector.
Two cursors, one per input slice.
While both slices still have elements...
...compare the fronts; `<=` keeps the merge stable.
Take from `a` when it is not larger.
steps.explanation:
Comparing only the fronts of the two sorted inputs emitted `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` in a
single linear pass. This merge, applied recursively to halves, is the whole of merge
sort.

steps.title: Binary search by hand
steps.intro:
On a sorted slice, keep a half-open window `[lo, hi)` and inspect its midpoint. A
match returns the index; too small moves `lo` past the midpoint; too large pulls `hi`
down to it. The window halves every step, so the search is O(log n).
steps.prompt:
Search a sorted slice for a value that is present and one that is absent.

**Why:** each comparison rules out half of the remaining window, so even a large
sorted slice is searched in a handful of steps — logarithmic, not linear.
line_comments: `binary_search` finds `target` in a sorted slice, returning its index.
If the midpoint is the target...
If the midpoint is too small...
Otherwise the midpoint is too large...
Window emptied without a match: not found.
Prints `Some(3) None` — `7` is at index 3, `4` is absent.
steps.explanation:
The window halved on every comparison, finding `7` at index 3 and exhausting the
window for the absent `4` (giving `None`). Binary search trades a sorted-input
requirement for logarithmic lookups.

steps.title: Split a vector in half
steps.intro:
Merge sort first splits the input in two. `Vec::split_off(mid)` does exactly that:
it truncates the vector to `[0, mid)` and returns the removed tail `[mid, len)` as a
new `Vec` — the two halves the recursion will sort.
steps.prompt:
Split `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` at its midpoint and print both halves.

**Why:** `split_off` is the clean, allocation-light way to divide a `Vec` into the
two owned halves merge sort recurses on, with no manual index juggling.
line_comments: `split_off` keeps `[0, mid)` in `v` and returns the rest.
Prints `[1, 2] [3, 4, 5]` — the two halves merge sort recurses on.
steps.explanation:
`split_off(2)` left `[1, 2]` in `v` and returned `[3, 4, 5]`. Dividing the input into
two owned halves is the first move of merge sort, before each half is sorted and merged.

steps.title: Implement merge sort
steps.intro:
Put the pieces together. Implement `merge_sort(v)`: split the vector in half,
recursively sort each half, and merge the two sorted halves back into one. The result
is a stable, ascending sort in O(n log n) — all from the merge and the split you
already built, with no call to `slice::sort`.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Sort a vector with merge sort:

```rust
pub fn merge_sort(mut v: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<i32> { ... }
```

Return a sorted (ascending, stable) copy of `v`. Split at the midpoint, sort each
half recursively, and merge the halves.

Rules:

- Do **not** use `slice::sort` or `sort_unstable` — write the merge yourself.
- A slice of length 0 or 1 is already sorted (the base case).
- The sort must be stable: keep equal elements in their original relative order
  (take from the left half on a tie with `<=`).

Examples:

- `merge_sort(vec![5, 1, 4, 2, 8])` → `vec![1, 2, 4, 5, 8]`
- `merge_sort(vec![])` → `vec![]`

**Hint:** if `v.len() <= 1` return `v`. Otherwise `let right = v.split_off(v.len() /
2);`, recurse on both parts, then merge them with two cursors, pushing the smaller
front each step and appending the leftovers.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The recursion halves the input at each level, giving **O(log n)** levels, and each
level merges a total of `n` elements in linear time, so the sort is **O(n log n)**. The
merge allocates a buffer proportional to the slice it combines, so auxiliary space is
**O(n)**. Taking from the left half on ties (`<=`) preserves the original order of
equal elements, so the sort is stable; the base case (length 0 or 1) is already sorted.

units.title: Recursion and Dynamic Programming
units.intro:
Recursion expresses a problem in terms of smaller copies of itself — elegant, but it
can redo the same work exponentially. **Dynamic programming** fixes that by solving
each subproblem once and remembering the answer: top-down with a cache (memoisation),
or bottom-up by filling a table. This unit shows naive recursion, memoised recursion,
and a bottom-up table, then solves coin change with a DP table.

steps.title: Remember what you already solved
steps.intro:
Dynamic programming is just recursion with its repeated subproblems solved only
once. Whether you cache results top-down or fill a table bottom-up, the win is the
same: exponential work collapses to polynomial.

steps.title: Naive recursive Fibonacci
steps.intro:
The direct recursion reads like the definition: `fib(n)` is `fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`,
with `0` and `1` as base cases. It is correct but wasteful — each call re-expands the
same subproblems, so the work grows exponentially with `n`.
steps.prompt:
Compute `fib(10)` with plain recursion.

**Why:** the naive version recomputes `fib` of the same arguments again and again; it
is fine for small `n` but motivates the memoisation that comes next.
line_comments: Prints `55` — but this recomputes subproblems exponentially.
steps.explanation:
The recursion matched the definition and gave `fib(10) = 55`, but it recomputed the
same smaller values many times. For large `n` that waste is fatal — which is exactly
what memoisation removes.

steps.title: Memoised Fibonacci
steps.intro:
A cache is all it takes. Before computing `fib(n)`, check whether `memo[n]` already
holds the answer; if so return it, otherwise compute, store, and return. Each
distinct `n` is solved exactly once, turning exponential work into linear.
steps.prompt:
Compute `fib(50)` using a `Vec<Option<u64>>` cache.

**Why:** memoisation solves each subproblem a single time; with the cache `fib(50)`
is instant, whereas the naive version would make billions of calls.
line_comments: Memoized Fibonacci: the cache turns exponential work into linear.
If this value is already cached...
...sum of the two predecessors (each itself memoized).
Store the result in the cache.
Prints `12586269025` — fast, because each subproblem is solved once.
steps.explanation:
The cache made each `fib(n)` compute only once, so `fib(50) = 12586269025` returned
instantly. That single change — remember what you solved — is the essence of dynamic
programming.

steps.title: Bottom-up coin table
steps.intro:
Tabulation builds the answer from the ground up. `dp[a]` is the fewest coins to make
amount `a`; start every entry at an "unreachable" marker, set `dp[0] = 0`, then for
each amount try each coin, improving `dp[a]` from the already-known `dp[a - c]`.
steps.prompt:
Find the fewest coins from `[1, 3, 4]` that make amount `6`, bottom-up.

**Why:** the fewest coins for `a` builds directly on the fewest for the smaller
amount `a - c`, so filling the table from `0` upward solves each amount exactly once.
line_comments: `dp[a]` = fewest coins to make `a`; start every entry at `unreachable`.
Build the table from `1` up to `amount`...
...only if it fits and `a - c` is itself reachable.
steps.explanation:
Each amount's answer was built from a smaller, already-solved amount, filling the
table up to `dp[6] = 2` (that is `3 + 3`). This bottom-up table is exactly the shape
of the coin-change challenge.

steps.title: Coin change
steps.intro:
The capstone of the track. Implement `coin_change(coins, amount)`: return the fewest
coins (any denomination, reused freely) that sum to exactly `amount`, or `None` if it
cannot be made. A bottom-up DP table holds the fewest coins for every amount from `0`
up to the target — each built from a smaller amount you have already solved.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Make an amount with the fewest coins:

```rust
pub fn coin_change(coins: &[u32], amount: u32) -> Option<u32> { ... }
```

Return `Some(k)` where `k` is the minimum number of coins from `coins` (each usable
any number of times) that sum to exactly `amount`, or `None` if no combination works.

Rules:

- `amount` of `0` needs `0` coins → `Some(0)`.
- If the amount cannot be formed (including when `coins` is empty and `amount > 0`),
  return `None`.
- Use a bottom-up DP table, not brute-force enumeration.

Examples:

- `coin_change(&[1, 2, 5], 11)` → `Some(3)` (5 + 5 + 1)
- `coin_change(&[2], 3)` → `None`
- `coin_change(&[1, 2, 5], 0)` → `Some(0)`

**Hint:** make `dp` of length `amount + 1`, every entry an "unreachable" marker
(`u32::MAX`) except `dp[0] = 0`. For each amount `a` from `1` to `amount`, for each
coin `c <= a` with `dp[a - c]` reachable, set `dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)`. The
answer is `dp[amount]`, or `None` if it stayed unreachable.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The table has `amount + 1` entries and each is relaxed against every coin, so the time
is **O(amount * coins)** and the space is **O(amount)**. `dp[a]` is the provably fewest
coins for amount `a`: it is built only from `dp[a - c]`, a strictly smaller amount that
is already final, so optimal substructure holds. An entry that never improves past the
`u32::MAX` marker is unreachable, which is reported as `None`; `dp[0] = 0` seeds the
base case.
